title: Judges

stories.title: ⚔️ Judges 1
summaryBullets: After the death of Joshua, the Israelites inquired of the LORD, “Who will be the first to go up and fight for us against the Canaanites?” (1:1).
“Judah shall go up,” answered the LORD. “Indeed, I have delivered the land into their hands.” (1:2).

Then the men of Judah said to their brothers the Simeonites, “Come up with us to our allotted territory, and let us fight against the Canaanites. And we likewise will go with you to your territory.” So the Simeonites went with them. (1:3).
When Judah attacked, the LORD delivered the Canaanites and Perizzites into their hands, and they struck down ten thousand men at Bezek. (1:4).
And there they found Adoni-bezek and fought against him, striking down the Canaanites and Perizzites. (1:5).
As Adoni-bezek fled, they pursued him, seized him, and cut off his thumbs and big toes. (1:6).

Then Adoni-bezek said, “Seventy kings with their thumbs and big toes cut off have gathered the scraps under my table. As I have done to them, so God has repaid me.” And they brought him to Jerusalem, where he died. (1:7).
Then the men of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it. They put the city to the sword and set it on fire. (1:8).
Afterward, the men of Judah marched down to fight against the Canaanites living in the hill country, in the Negev, and in the foothills. (1:9).
Judah also marched against the Canaanites who were living in Hebron (formerly known as Kiriath-arba), and they struck down Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai. (1:10).
From there they marched against the inhabitants of Debir (formerly known as Kiriath-sepher). (1:11).
And Caleb said, “To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage.” (1:12).
So Othniel son of Caleb’s younger brother Kenaz captured the city, and Caleb gave his daughter Acsah to him in marriage. (1:13).
One day Acsah came to Othniel and urged him to ask her father for a field. When she got off her donkey, Caleb asked her, “What do you desire?” (1:14).
“Give me a blessing,” she answered. “Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me springs of water as well.” So Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs. (1:15).

Now the descendants of Moses’ father-in-law, the Kenite, went up with the men of Judah from the City of Palms to the Wilderness of Judah in the Negev near Arad. They went to live among the people. (1:16).
Then the men of Judah went with their brothers the Simeonites, attacked the Canaanites living in Zephath, and devoted the city to destruction. So it was called Hormah. (1:17).
And Judah also captured Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron — each with its territory. (1:18).
The LORD was with Judah, and they took possession of the hill country; but they could not drive out the inhabitants of the plains because they had chariots of iron. (1:19).
Just as Moses had promised, Judah gave Hebron to Caleb, who drove out the descendants of the three sons of Anak. (1:20).
The Benjamites, however, failed to drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem. So to this day the Jebusites live there among the Benjamites. (1:21).
The house of Joseph also attacked Bethel, and the LORD was with them. (1:22).
They sent spies to Bethel (formerly known as Luz), (1:23).
and when the spies saw a man coming out of the city, they said to him, “Please show us how to get into the city, and we will treat you kindly.” (1:24).
So the man showed them the entrance to the city, and they put the city to the sword but released that man and all his family. (1:25).
And the man went to the land of the Hittites, built a city, and called it Luz, which is its name to this day. (1:26).
At that time Manasseh failed to drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, Megiddo, and their villages; for the Canaanites were determined to dwell in that land. (1:27).
When Israel became stronger, they pressed the Canaanites into forced labor, but they never drove them out completely. (1:28).
Ephraim also failed to drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer; so the Canaanites continued to dwell among them in Gezer. (1:29).
Zebulun failed to drive out the inhabitants of Kitron and Nahalol; so the Canaanites lived among them and served as forced laborers. (1:30).
Asher failed to drive out the inhabitants of Acco, Sidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, and Rehob. (1:31).
So the Asherites lived among the Canaanite inhabitants of the land, because they did not drive them out. (1:32).

Naphtali failed to drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath. So the Naphtalites also lived among the Canaanite inhabitants of the land, but the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath served them as forced laborers. (1:33).
The Amorites forced the Danites into the hill country and did not allow them to come down into the plain. (1:34).
And the Amorites were determined to dwell in Mount Heres, Aijalon, and Shaalbim. But when the house of Joseph grew in strength, they pressed the Amorites into forced labor. (1:35).
And the border of the Amorites extended from the Ascent of Akrabbim to Sela and beyond. (1:36).
crossRefs: Joshua 15:13-19: Caleb takes Hebron and Debir, and his daughter Achsah asks him for the upper and lower springs.
Joshua 13:1-6: Joshua is old, and the land that still remains to be taken is listed region by region.
Exodus 23:31-33: I will give the inhabitants into your hand; make no covenant with them or with their gods.
Joshua 17:12-13: Manasseh could not take those towns, and when Israel grew strong it put the Canaanites to forced labour instead.
Judges 2:1-3: The angel at Bochim says the nations left in the land will be thorns in your sides and their gods a snare to you.

translationNotes.term: Thumbs and big toes cut off
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֹּהֶן (bohen), thumb or big toe
translationNotes.note: Verses 6 and 7 report a mutilation with a military purpose. A man without thumbs cannot grip a sword or draw a bow, and a man without big toes cannot run or hold his footing, so it disables a warrior for life while leaving him alive to be looked at. Adoni-bezek says he had done it to seventy kings and made them pick scraps up off the floor under his table, and he reads what is done to him as the same account settled.

Verse 16 brings in the family of Moses' father-in-law, who came up from the City of Palms, meaning Jericho, and settled in the dry country near Arad. They were a small people who moved with their tents and lived alongside Israel without being part of it. Jael, who kills Sisera, is the wife of a Kenite (4:17), and Saul warns the Kenites to get clear of Amalek before he attacks because they had shown Israel kindness at the exodus (1 Samuel 15:6).

translationNotes.term: The man who showed the way into Bethel
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָבוֹא הָעִיר (mavo ha-ir), the entrance of the city
translationNotes.note: Verses 23 to 26 turn on one man giving away the way in. A walled town had one gate that was shut at dark, and any second entrance, a postern, a drain, a weak stretch of wall, was known only to those who lived there. He and his household are spared for it, which is the same bargain Rahab made at Jericho, and he then goes off to Hittite country and founds a new town under the old name, Luz.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעֲלֵה עַקְרַבִּים (Maaleh Aqrabbim), the scorpion ascent
translationNotes.note: Verse 36 fixes the Amorite border at the Ascent of Akrabbim, which means the scorpion pass: the steep climb out of the Arabah at the southern end of the Dead Sea up onto the Negev plateau. It is the fixed southern boundary of the land in Numbers 34:4 and Joshua 15:3. Naming a pass after the creature that infests it was ordinary, and it tells a traveller what to expect.

stories.keyTakeaway: After Joshua's death, Judah and Simeon attack the Canaanites and capture several cities including Jerusalem and Hebron, though some tribes fail to fully drive out their enemies and instead reduce them to forced labor.

headings.text: The Capture of Jerusalem and Hebron
The Failure to Complete the Conquest

stories.title: ⚔️ Judges 2
summaryBullets: Now the angel of the LORD went up from Gilgal to Bochim and said, “I brought you up out of Egypt and led you into the land that I had promised to your fathers, and I said, ‘I will never break My covenant with you, (2:1).
and you are not to make a covenant with the people of this land, but you shall tear down their altars.’ Yet you have not obeyed My voice. What is this you have done? (2:2).
So now I tell you that I will not drive out these people before you; they will be thorns in your sides, and their gods will be a snare to you.” (2:3).
When the angel of the LORD had spoken these words to all the Israelites, the people lifted up their voices and wept. (2:4).
So they called that place Bochim and offered sacrifices there to the LORD. (2:5).
After Joshua had dismissed the people, the Israelites went out to take possession of the land, each to his own inheritance. (2:6).
And the people served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him, who had seen all the great works that the LORD had done for Israel. (2:7).
And Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110. (2:8).
They buried him in the land of his inheritance, at Timnath-heres in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash. (2:9).
After that whole generation had also been gathered to their fathers, another generation rose up who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel. (2:10).
And the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals. (2:11).

Thus they forsook the LORD, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt, and they followed after various gods of the peoples around them. They bowed down to them and provoked the LORD to anger, (2:12).
for they forsook Him and served Baal and the Ashtoreths. (2:13).

Then the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He delivered them into the hands of those who plundered them. He sold them into the hands of their enemies all around, whom they were no longer able to resist. (2:14).
Wherever Israel marched out, the hand of the LORD was against them to bring calamity, just as He had sworn to them. So they were greatly distressed. (2:15).
Then the LORD raised up judges, who saved them from the hands of those who plundered them. (2:16).

Israel, however, did not listen to their judges. Instead, they prostituted themselves with other gods and bowed down to them. They quickly turned from the way of their fathers, who had walked in obedience to the LORD’s commandments; they did not do as their fathers had done. (2:17).

Whenever the LORD raised up a judge for the Israelites, He was with that judge and saved them from the hands of their enemies while the judge was still alive; for the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning under those who oppressed them and afflicted them. (2:18).

But when the judge died, the Israelites became even more corrupt than their fathers, going after other gods to serve them and bow down to them. They would not give up their evil practices and stubborn ways. (2:19).
So the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He said, “Because this nation has transgressed the covenant I laid down for their fathers and has not heeded My voice, (2:20).
I will no longer drive out before them any of the nations Joshua left when he died. (2:21).
In this way I will test whether Israel will keep the way of the LORD by walking in it as their fathers did.” (2:22).
That is why the LORD had left those nations in place and had not driven them out immediately by delivering them into the hand of Joshua. (2:23).
crossRefs: Joshua 24:29-31: Joshua dies at a hundred and ten and is buried at Timnath-serah, and Israel served the LORD all his days.
Deuteronomy 7:1-5: Devote them to destruction, make no covenant with them, and tear down their altars, pillars, and Asherim.
Exodus 34:12-16: Make no covenant with the inhabitants of the land, or their daughters will draw your sons after their gods.
Numbers 33:55: If you do not drive out the inhabitants, those you let remain will be barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides.
Psalm 106:34-42: They did not destroy the peoples, but mixed with the nations, learned their works, and served their idols.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּעַל (baal), lord or master; plural בְּעָלִים (bealim) - עַשְׁתָּרוֹת (Ashtaroth)
translationNotes.note: Baal means lord or master, and he was the Canaanite storm god, held to send the rain that every harvest depended on; the plural in verse 11, the Baals, reflects the fact that each locality had its own. His worship ran on the farming year, and his prophets on Carmel cut themselves with swords and lances until the blood ran (1 Kings 18:28). Ashtoreth, plural Ashtaroth, was the goddess set beside him, named at 1 Kings 11:5 as the goddess of the Sidonians and served with sexual rites; the Philistines put Saul's armour in her temple (1 Samuel 31:10). Verse 13 says Israel forsook the LORD and served both.

Malakh means one who is sent, a messenger, and the word is used of human couriers as readily as of heavenly ones; the Greek angelos behind the English angel means the same thing. In verse 1 the messenger comes up from Gilgal to Bochim and speaks in the first person as God, saying I brought you up out of Egypt and I will never break My covenant with you. The same figure appears to Gideon (6:11-22) and to Manoah and his wife (13:3-21), and in each case the person addressed reacts as though he has met God Himself.

The place gets its name in verse 5 from what happened there, which is how a great many places in Scripture are named. Israel hears the charge, weeps, and sacrifices, and the site carries the word for weeping from then on. The same pattern names Bethel, Beersheba, Massah, Meribah, and the Valley of Achor.

A shofet was not a courtroom official. The word covers ruling and setting things right, and in this book it names a deliverer raised up for a particular crisis who then led that part of Israel for the rest of his life. None of them was elected, none inherited the office, and none ruled the whole nation. The book covers roughly three centuries between Joshua and Samuel.

translationNotes.term: Played the harlot after other gods
translationNotes.note: Verse 17 does not say Israel experimented with other religions; it uses zanah, the ordinary verb for prostitution, and applies it to the nation. The image runs right through the prophets, most of all in Hosea, because the covenant at Sinai was framed as a marriage bond with exclusive claims. The word is chosen to say that this is betrayal of a person, not a change of opinion.

stories.keyTakeaway: The angel of the LORD rebukes Israel at Bokim for breaking covenant and disobeying his commands; after Joshua's death, a new generation abandons the LORD for foreign gods, prompting him to give them over to raiders and establish a cycle where judges save them temporarily but they return to idolatry after each judge dies.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judges 3
summaryBullets: These are the nations that the LORD left to test all the Israelites who had not known any of the wars in Canaan, (3:1).
if only to teach warfare to the subsequent generations of Israel, especially to those who had not known it formerly: (3:2).
the five rulers of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who lived in the mountains of Lebanon from Mount Baal-hermon to Lebo-hamath. (3:3).
These nations were left to test the Israelites, to find out whether they would keep the commandments of the LORD, which He had given their fathers through Moses. (3:4).
Thus the Israelites continued to live among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. (3:5).
And they took the daughters of these people in marriage, gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods. (3:6).
So the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD; they forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asherahs. (3:7).
Then the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram-naharaim, and the Israelites served him eight years. (3:8).
But when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up Othniel son of Caleb’s younger brother Kenaz as a deliverer to save them. (3:9).

The Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he became Israel’s judge and went out to war. And the LORD delivered Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram into the hand of Othniel, who prevailed against him. (3:10).
So the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died. (3:11).
Once again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD. So He gave Eglon king of Moab power over Israel, because they had done evil in the sight of the LORD. (3:12).
After enlisting the Ammonites and Amalekites to join forces with him, Eglon attacked and defeated Israel, taking possession of the City of Palms. (3:13).
The Israelites served Eglon king of Moab eighteen years. (3:14).
And again they cried out to the LORD, and He raised up Ehud son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite, as their deliverer. So they sent him with tribute to Eglon king of Moab. (3:15).
Now Ehud had made for himself a double-edged sword a cubit long. He strapped it to his right thigh under his cloak (3:16).
and brought the tribute to Eglon king of Moab, who was an obese man. (3:17).
After Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he ushered out those who had carried it. (3:18).
But upon reaching the idols near Gilgal, he himself turned back and said, “I have a secret message for you, O king.” “Silence,” said the king, and all his attendants left him. (3:19).
Then Ehud approached him while he was sitting alone in the coolness of his upper room. “I have a word from God for you,” Ehud said, and the king rose from his seat. (3:20).
And Ehud reached with his left hand, pulled the sword from his right thigh, and plunged it into Eglon’s belly. (3:21).
Even the handle sank in after the blade, and Eglon’s fat closed in over it, so that Ehud did not withdraw the sword from his belly. And Eglon’s bowels emptied. (3:22).
Then Ehud went out through the porch, closing and locking the doors of the upper room behind him. (3:23).
After Ehud was gone, Eglon’s servants came in and found the doors of the upper room locked. “He must be relieving himself in the cool room,” they said. (3:24).

So they waited until they became worried and saw that he had still not opened the doors of the upper room. Then they took the key and opened the doors— and there was their lord lying dead on the floor. (3:25).
Ehud, however, had escaped while the servants waited. He passed by the idols and escaped to Seirah. (3:26).
On arriving in Seirah, he blew the ram’s horn throughout the hill country of Ephraim. The Israelites came down with him from the hills, and he became their leader. (3:27).

“Follow me,” he told them, “for the LORD has delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand.” So they followed him down and seized the fords of the Jordan leading to Moab, and they did not allow anyone to cross over. (3:28).
At that time they struck down about ten thousand Moabites, all robust and valiant men. Not one of them escaped. (3:29).
So Moab was subdued under the hand of Israel that day, and the land had rest for eighty years. (3:30).
After Ehud came Shamgar son of Anath. And he too saved Israel, striking down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad. (3:31).
crossRefs: Joshua 13:2-6: The land that still remained, including the five Philistine lords, the Sidonians, and the Lebanon.
Judges 1:12-13: Othniel takes Kiriath-sepher and receives Achsah, Caleb's daughter, as his wife.
Deuteronomy 8:2-3: God led you forty years in the wilderness to humble you and to test you, to know what was in your heart.
Numbers 22:1: Israel camps in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho, the country Eglon holds in this chapter.
1 Samuel 13:19-22: The Philistines allowed no smith in Israel, the world in which an oxgoad becomes a weapon.

translationNotes.term: Bound as to his right hand
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew behind left-handed in verse 15 says bound, or restricted, as to his right hand. It matters tactically: a sword was worn on the left hip to be drawn across the body by the right hand, so a guard searching an envoy would check the left side. Ehud straps an eighteen-inch blade to his right thigh under his cloak and walks into an audience with it. The same phrase describes the seven hundred picked slingers of Benjamin at 20:16, and Benjamin means son of the right hand.

The distance from elbow to fingertip; about 18 inches (45 cm). The standard biblical measure for buildings (Noah's ark, the tabernacle, Solomon's temple) and bodies. Goliath was 'six cubits and a span' tall, about 9 feet 9 in. A 'long cubit' (Ezekiel 40:5) added a handbreadth.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲלִיַּת הַמְּקֵרָה (aliyyat ha-meqerah), the roof chamber of cooling
translationNotes.note: Verses 20 to 25 all happen in a room built on the flat roof of the house, reached by its own stair and open to the breeze; it was the coolest and most private room a wealthy man had, which is why the king takes a confidential message there alone. When the servants find the doors locked they assume he is relieving himself, which is what the Hebrew idiom in verse 24 says without saying, and they wait until they are embarrassed. That delay is Ehud's head start.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲרַם נַהֲרַיִם (Aram Naharayim), Aram of the two rivers
translationNotes.note: Verse 8 names Israel's first oppressor in the book and the country he came from. Aram-naharaim means Aram of the two rivers, the upper Mesopotamian country between the Euphrates and its tributary the Habur, the same region Abraham's family came from and where Isaac's bride was found (Genesis 24:10). The king's name as it stands in Hebrew reads Cushan of double wickedness.

Verse 31 has Shamgar kill six hundred Philistines with a goad. A goad was a pole roughly eight feet long with an iron point at one end for driving plough oxen and a flat blade at the other for scraping the ploughshare clean. It was a farm tool, and under Philistine rule it was one of the few iron-tipped things an Israelite farmer was allowed to own; 1 Samuel 13:20-21 has Israelites going down to the Philistines even to get their goads sharpened.

stories.keyTakeaway: God leaves pagan nations in Canaan to test Israel's obedience; when Israel intermarries with them and worships their gods, God delivers them into oppression, then raises up judges - first Othniel against Aram, then Ehud who assassinates Moab's King Eglon and leads Israel to victory, and finally Shamgar who kills six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad.

stories.title: 🪓 Judges 4
summaryBullets: After Ehud died, the Israelites again did evil in the sight of the LORD. (4:1).
So the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his forces was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim. (4:2).
Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD, because Jabin had nine hundred chariots of iron, and he had harshly oppressed the Israelites for twenty years. (4:3).
Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time. (4:4).
And she would sit under the Palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, where the Israelites would go up to her for judgment. (4:5).

She summoned Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali and said to him, “Surely the LORD, the God of Israel, is commanding you: ‘Go and march to Mount Tabor, taking with you ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun. (4:6).
And I will draw out Sisera the commander of Jabin’s army, his chariots, and his troops to the River Kishon, and I will deliver him into your hand.’” (4:7).
Barak said to her, “If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go.” (4:8).

“I will certainly go with you,” Deborah replied, “but the road you are taking will bring you no honor, because the LORD will be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman.” So Deborah got up and went with Barak to Kedesh, (4:9).
where he summoned Zebulun and Naphtali. Ten thousand men followed him, and Deborah also went with him. (4:10).
Now Heber the Kenite had moved away from the Kenites, the descendants of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses, and had pitched his tent by the great tree of Zaanannim, which was near Kedesh. (4:11).
When Sisera was told that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up Mount Tabor, (4:12).
he summoned all nine hundred of his iron chariots and all the men with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the River Kishon. (4:13).

Then Deborah said to Barak, “Arise, for this is the day that the LORD has delivered Sisera into your hand. Has not the LORD gone before you?” So Barak came down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men following him. (4:14).
And in front of him the LORD routed with the sword Sisera, all his charioteers, and all his army. Sisera abandoned his chariot and fled on foot. (4:15).
Then Barak pursued the chariots and army as far as Harosheth-hagoyim, and the whole army of Sisera fell by the sword; not a single man was left. (4:16).
Meanwhile, Sisera had fled on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, because there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite. (4:17).
Jael went out to greet Sisera and said to him, “Come in, my lord. Come in with me. Do not be afraid.” So he entered her tent, and she covered him with a blanket. (4:18).
Sisera said to her, “Please give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty.” So she opened a container of milk, gave him a drink, and covered him again. (4:19).
“Stand at the entrance to the tent,” he said, “and if anyone comes and asks you, ‘Is there a man here?’ say, ‘No.’” (4:20).

But as he lay sleeping from exhaustion, Heber’s wife Jael took a tent peg, grabbed a hammer, and went silently to Sisera. She drove the peg through his temple and into the ground, and he died. (4:21).

When Barak arrived in pursuit of Sisera, Jael went out to greet him and said to him, “Come, and I will show you the man you are seeking.” So he went in with her, and there lay Sisera dead, with a tent peg through his temple. (4:22).
On that day God subdued Jabin king of Canaan before the Israelites. (4:23).
And the hand of the Israelites grew stronger and stronger against Jabin king of Canaan until they destroyed him. (4:24).
crossRefs: Joshua 11:1-9: Jabin king of Hazor leads a northern coalition with horses and chariots and is defeated at the waters of Merom.
Exodus 15:20-21: Miriam the prophetess takes a tambourine and leads the women out with singing after the sea.
Judges 5:1-31: The song of Deborah and Barak, telling the same battle in verse.
1 Samuel 12:9-11: Samuel names Sisera among the enemies Israel was sold to, and the deliverers God sent them.
Psalm 83:9-10: Do to them as You did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the river Kishon.

translationNotes.note: A neviah is a woman who speaks for God, and the office is not rare in Scripture: Miriam (Exodus 15:20), Huldah, who authenticates the book of the law for King Josiah (2 Kings 22:14), and Anna in the temple (Luke 2:36). Verse 4 gives Deborah both roles at once, prophetess and judge, and verses 6 and 7 have her deliver Barak's orders as a word already given by the LORD, down to the place and the numbers.

Verse 5 says she sat under a particular palm tree between Ramah and Bethel and Israel came up to her for judgment. Sitting was the posture for giving a ruling, and a named landmark tree served as a fixed public place in country where there was no courthouse; elsewhere the elders sat in the town gate. That she holds court on the ridge road between two towns, and men travel to her, is the measure of her standing before Barak is ever mentioned.

A war chariot was wood, so calling them iron means iron fittings and tyres, the newer and stronger technology. They needed level ground, which is why Israel held the hills and the Canaanites held the valleys (Judges 1:19). Sisera brings them out onto the flat floor of the Jezreel valley, which is exactly where chariots win and exactly where the Kishon in flood destroys them (Judges 5:21).

In a nomadic household the women pitched and struck the tents, so a peg and a mallet were tools Jael used every day and handled better than most men. Verse 21 has her drive it through his temple while he sleeps. The detail is not a lucky improvisation; it is the weapon nearest her hand and one she knew how to swing.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel again does evil and is oppressed by Jabin's commander Sisera for twenty years until Deborah, a prophet judging Israel, sends Barak to fight him at Mount Tabor. The LORD routes Sisera's army; Sisera flees to Jael's tent, where she kills him with a tent peg while he sleeps, and Israel's pressure against Jabin intensifies.

stories.title: 🪓 Judges 5
summaryBullets: On that day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang this song: (5:1).
“When the princes take the lead in Israel, when the people volunteer, bless the LORD. (5:2).
Listen, O kings! Give ear, O princes! I will sing to the LORD; I will sing praise to the LORD, the God of Israel. (5:3).
O LORD, when You went out from Seir, when You marched from the land of Edom, the earth trembled, the heavens poured out rain, and the clouds poured down water. (5:4).
The mountains quaked before the LORD, the One of Sinai, before the LORD, the God of Israel. (5:5).
In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were deserted and the travelers took the byways. (5:6).
Life in the villages ceased; it ended in Israel, until I, Deborah, arose, a mother in Israel. (5:7).
When they chose new gods, then war came to their gates. Not a shield or spear was found among forty thousand in Israel. (5:8).
My heart is with the princes of Israel, with the volunteers among the people. Bless the LORD! (5:9).
You who ride white donkeys, who sit on saddle blankets, and you who travel the road, ponder (5:10).

the voices of the singers at the watering places. There they shall recount the righteous acts of the LORD, the righteous deeds of His villagers in Israel. Then the people of the LORD went down to the gates: (5:11).
‘Awake, awake, O Deborah! Awake, awake, sing a song! Arise, O Barak, and take hold of your captives, O son of Abinoam!’ (5:12).
Then the survivors came down to the nobles; the people of the LORD came down to me against the mighty. (5:13).
Some came from Ephraim, with their roots in Amalek; Benjamin came with your people after you. The commanders came down from Machir, the bearers of the marshal’s staff from Zebulun. (5:14).
The princes of Issachar were with Deborah, and Issachar was with Barak, rushing into the valley at his heels. In the clans of Reuben there was great indecision. (5:15).
Why did you sit among the sheepfolds to hear the whistling for the flocks? In the clans of Reuben there was great indecision. (5:16).
Gilead remained beyond the Jordan. Dan, why did you linger by the ships? Asher stayed at the coast and remained in his harbors. (5:17).
Zebulun was a people who risked their lives; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the battlefield. (5:18).
Kings came and fought; then the kings of Canaan fought at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo, but they took no plunder of silver. (5:19).
From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera. (5:20).
The River Kishon swept them away, the ancient river, the River Kishon. March on, O my soul, in strength! (5:21).
Then the hooves of horses thundered— the mad galloping of his stallions. (5:22).
‘Curse Meroz,’ says the angel of the LORD. ‘Bitterly curse her inhabitants; for they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty.’ (5:23).
Most blessed among women is Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, most blessed of tent-dwelling women. (5:24).
He asked for water, and she gave him milk. In a magnificent bowl she brought him curds. (5:25).
She reached for the tent peg, her right hand for the workman’s hammer. She struck Sisera and crushed his skull; she shattered and pierced his temple. (5:26).
At her feet he collapsed, he fell, there he lay still; at her feet he collapsed, he fell; where he collapsed, there he fell dead. (5:27).
Sisera’s mother looked through the window; she peered through the lattice and lamented: ‘Why is his chariot so long in coming? What has delayed the clatter of his chariots?’ (5:28).
Her wisest ladies answer; indeed she keeps telling herself, (5:29).
‘Are they not finding and dividing the spoil— a girl or two for each warrior, a plunder of dyed garments for Sisera, the spoil of embroidered garments for the neck of the looter?’ (5:30).
So may all Your enemies perish, O LORD! But may those who love You shine like the sun at its brightest.” And the land had rest for forty years. (5:31).
crossRefs: Judges 4:1-24: The same battle told as narrative, with Sisera fleeing on foot to Jael's tent.
Exodus 15:1-18: The song at the sea after Egypt's army is drowned, the earlier victory song of the same kind.
Deuteronomy 33:2: The LORD came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon them; He shone forth from Mount Paran.
Psalm 68:7-8: When You went out before Your people and marched through the wilderness, the earth quaked and the heavens poured down rain.
Habakkuk 3:3-6: God comes from Teman; the mountains see Him and writhe, and the everlasting hills sink low.

translationNotes.note: Verse 6 says travellers took the winding byways and life in the villages stopped, which is the plain description of a country where the main roads are not safe. Verse 8 adds that no shield or spear was to be seen among forty thousand in Israel. Between them the two lines describe an occupied population, disarmed and unable to move goods, and it is the same condition the Philistines later impose in 1 Samuel 13:19-22.

Verse 25 sharpens verse 4:19. Sisera asked for water and Jael gave him milk, and the song says she brought curds in a bowl fit for a nobleman. Chemah is soured, thickened milk, the ordinary drink and food of tent-dwellers, and it is what Abraham sets before his three visitors (Genesis 18:8). Giving a fugitive food and drink in your tent was the act that placed him under your protection, which is what makes verse 26 land.

translationNotes.term: The mother of Sisera at the window
translationNotes.note: Verses 28 to 30 put Sisera's mother at a latticed window counting the reasons his chariots are late, and the song lets her wise ladies say out loud what everyone expected the victors to be dividing. The Hebrew of verse 30 is blunter than most translations: it counts the spoil as a womb or two for each man, then the dyed cloth. Rape and the taking of captive women were understood as part of what an army carried home, and the song says so without softening it.

The Kishon drains the whole Jezreel valley westward to the sea past Mount Carmel. For most of the year it is a shallow stream in a flat clay plain; in a heavy downpour that plain turns to mud and the channel becomes a torrent. Verses 4, 20, and 21 describe rain, and a chariot army on soft ground is a stranded army.

Verse 23 has the angel of the LORD curse Meroz bitterly because its people did not come to the help of the LORD against the mighty. The town is named nowhere else in Scripture and its site is not known. The song lists who came, who stayed among the sheepfolds, and who was cursed for it, and Meroz is the one that gets a curse rather than a shrug.

stories.keyTakeaway: Deborah and Barak sing a song recounting the victory over Sisera's forces, praising the tribes that fought, cursing Meroz for not helping, honoring Jael for killing Sisera, and mocking Sisera's mother waiting for his return.

headings.text: The Song of Deborah and Barak

stories.title: 🔥 Judges 6
summaryBullets: Again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD; so He delivered them into the hand of Midian for seven years, (6:1).
and the hand of Midian prevailed against Israel. Because of the Midianites, the Israelites prepared shelters for themselves in the mountains, caves, and strongholds. (6:2).
Whenever the Israelites planted their crops, the Midianites, Amalekites, and other people of the east would come up and invade them, (6:3).
encamping against them as far as Gaza and destroying the produce of the land. They left Israel with no sustenance, neither sheep nor oxen nor donkeys. (6:4).
For the Midianites came with their livestock and their tents like a great swarm of locusts. They and their camels were innumerable, and they entered the land to ravage it. (6:5).
Israel was greatly impoverished by Midian, and the Israelites cried out to the LORD. (6:6).
Now when the Israelites cried out to the LORD because of Midian, (6:7).
He sent them a prophet, who told them, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I brought you up out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. (6:8).
I delivered you out of the hands of Egypt and all your oppressors. I drove them out before you and gave you their land. (6:9).
And I said to you: ‘I am the LORD your God. You must not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell.’ But you did not obey Me.” (6:10).

Then the angel of the LORD came and sat down under the oak in Ophrah that belonged to Joash the Abiezrite, where his son Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites. (6:11).
And the angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon and said, “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor.” (6:12).

“Please, my Lord,” Gideon replied, “if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us? And where are all His wonders of which our fathers told us, saying, ‘Has not the LORD brought us up out of Egypt?’ But now the LORD has forsaken us and delivered us into the hand of Midian.” (6:13).
The LORD turned to him and said, “Go in the strength you have and save Israel from the hand of Midian. Am I not sending you?” (6:14).
“Please, my Lord,” Gideon replied, “how can I save Israel? Indeed, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father’s house.” (6:15).
“Surely I will be with you,” the LORD replied, “and you will strike down all the Midianites as one man.” (6:16).
Gideon answered, “If I have found favor in Your sight, give me a sign that it is You speaking with me. (6:17).
Please do not depart from this place until I return to You. Let me bring my offering and set it before You.” And the LORD said, “I will stay until you return.” (6:18).

So Gideon went in and prepared a young goat and unleavened bread and an ephah of flour. He placed the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot and brought them out to present to Him under the oak. (6:19).
And the angel of God said to him, “Take the meat and the unleavened bread, lay them on this rock, and pour out the broth.” And Gideon did so. (6:20).

Then the angel of the LORD extended the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened bread. And fire flared from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened bread. Then the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight. (6:21).
When Gideon realized that it was the angel of the LORD, he said, “Oh no, Lord GOD! I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!” (6:22).
But the LORD said to him, “Peace be with you. Do not be afraid, for you will not die.” (6:23).
So Gideon built an altar to the LORD there and called it The LORD Is Peace. To this day it stands in Ophrah of the Abiezrites. (6:24).
On that very night the LORD said to Gideon, “Take your father’s young bull and a second bull seven years old, tear down your father’s altar to Baal, and cut down the Asherah pole beside it. (6:25).
Then build a proper altar to the LORD your God on the top of this stronghold. And with the wood of the Asherah pole you cut down, take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering.” (6:26).

So Gideon took ten of his servants and did as the LORD had told him. But because he was too afraid of his father’s household and the men of the city, he did it by night rather than in the daytime. (6:27).
When the men of the city got up in the morning, there was Baal’s altar torn down, with the Asherah pole cut down beside it and the second bull offered up on the newly built altar. (6:28).
“Who did this?” they said to one another. And after they had investigated thoroughly, they were told, “Gideon son of Joash did it.” (6:29).
Then the men of the city said to Joash, “Bring out your son. He must die, because he has torn down Baal’s altar and cut down the Asherah pole beside it.” (6:30).

But Joash said to all who stood against him, “Are you contending for Baal? Are you trying to save him? Whoever pleads his case will be put to death by morning! If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself with the one who has torn down his altar.” (6:31).
So on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal, that is to say, “Let Baal contend with him,” because he had torn down Baal’s altar. (6:32).
Then all the Midianites, Amalekites, and other people of the east gathered together, crossed over the Jordan, and camped in the Valley of Jezreel. (6:33).
So the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon, who blew the ram’s horn and rallied the Abiezrites behind him. (6:34).
Calling them to arms, Gideon sent messengers throughout Manasseh, as well as Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, so that they came up to meet him. (6:35).
Then Gideon said to God, “If You are going to save Israel by my hand, as You have said, (6:36).

then behold, I will place a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew only on the fleece and all the ground is dry, then I will know that You are going to save Israel by my hand, as You have said.” (6:37).
And that is what happened. When Gideon arose the next morning, he squeezed the fleece and wrung out the dew — a bowlful of water. (6:38).
Then Gideon said to God, “Do not be angry with me; let me speak one more time. Please allow me one more test with the fleece. This time let it be dry, and the ground covered with dew.” (6:39).
And that night God did so. Only the fleece was dry, and dew covered the ground. (6:40).
crossRefs: Genesis 37:25-28: Midianite traders come by with camels carrying spices, balm, and myrrh, and Joseph is sold to them.
Exodus 3:1-12: Moses at the burning bush is sent, and answers, who am I that I should go to Pharaoh.
Deuteronomy 7:5: Break down their altars, dash their pillars in pieces, cut down their Asherim, and burn their carved images.
Numbers 25:16-18: Israel is told to strike the Midianites, because they deceived Israel in the matter of Peor.
Exodus 33:20: You cannot see My face, for man shall not see Me and live.

translationNotes.note: Verse 32 explains the nickname from Joash's answer in verse 31: if Baal is a god, let him contend for himself with the man who tore down his altar. The name sticks, and the writer uses it for Gideon through chapters 7 to 9. Later scribes were uneasy carrying the name of Baal in an Israelite name at all, which is why 2 Samuel 11:21 calls the same man Jerubbesheth, swapping in bosheth, shame, the same substitution that turns Saul's son Eshbaal into Ish-bosheth.

Verses 25 to 28 have Gideon cut down the asherah standing next to his father's altar of Baal and burn a bull on the wood of it. Asherah was a goddess, and the asherah of the law is her cult object: a wooden pole or a living tree set up beside an altar, which is exactly what Deuteronomy 16:21 forbids planting next to the altar of the LORD. It appears again and again through the kings, and 2 Kings 21:7 has Manasseh put a carved image of Asherah inside the temple itself.
The standard Old Testament dry measure for grain, about 22 quarts or 5.8 gallons (22 liters). Ruth carries home an ephah of barley after a day's gleaning (Ruth 2:17).

A flat, hard, outdoor surface, usually a leveled rock or beaten-earth circle at the edge of town, where harvested grain was separated from chaff. Oxen pulled a wooden sledge over the stalks; the mixed kernels and chaff were then winnowed in the wind. Threshing floors doubled as public civic spaces (Ruth 3; 2 Samuel 24:18; Solomon's temple site).

Threshing needs an open, exposed floor and a breeze to carry the chaff away, which is why threshing floors sit on high ground outside a town. A winepress is the opposite: a pit cut down into rock with a channel to a lower vat, enclosed and out of sight. Verse 11 has Gideon beating out grain in one, and the picture tells you the situation before the angel says a word.

Verses 3 to 6 describe raiders arriving with their livestock and their tents once the crop was up, camping in the land, eating the harvest, and moving on. Camels let a raiding force cross desert that an army on foot could not and strike well beyond its own grazing range. Israel's answer in verse 2 was to live in the dens, caves, and strongholds of the hills.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Midianites oppress Israel for seven years until the people cry out; the angel of the LORD appears to Gideon at Ophrah, commissions him to save Israel, and confirms the call through fire consuming an offering. Gideon tears down his father's altar to Baal at night, receives the name Jerub-Baal, summons warriors from multiple tribes as the Spirit comes upon him, and requests two fleece signs from God, both of which occur as he asks.

stories.title: 🔥 Judges 7
summaryBullets: Early in the morning Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) and all the men with him camped beside the spring of Harod. And the camp of Midian was north of them in the valley near the hill of Moreh. (7:1).
Then the LORD said to Gideon, “You have too many men for Me to deliver Midian into their hands, lest Israel glorify themselves over Me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’ (7:2).

Now, therefore, proclaim in the hearing of the men: ‘Whoever is fearful and trembling may turn back and leave Mount Gilead.’” So twenty-two thousand of them turned back, but ten thousand remained. (7:3).

Then the LORD said to Gideon, “There are still too many men. Take them down to the water, and I will sift them for you there. If I say to you, ‘This one shall go with you,’ he shall go. But if I say, ‘This one shall not go with you,’ he shall not go.” (7:4).
So Gideon brought the men down to the water, and the LORD said to him, “Separate those who lap the water with their tongues like a dog from those who kneel to drink.” (7:5).
And the number of those who lapped the water with their hands to their mouths was three hundred men; all the others knelt to drink. (7:6).
Then the LORD said to Gideon, “With the three hundred men who lapped the water I will save you and deliver the Midianites into your hand. But all the others are to go home.” (7:7).

So Gideon sent the rest of the Israelites to their tents but kept the three hundred men, who took charge of the provisions and rams’ horns of the others. And the camp of Midian lay below him in the valley. (7:8).
That night the LORD said to Gideon, “Get up and go down against the camp, for I have delivered it into your hand. (7:9).
But if you are afraid to do so, then go down to the camp with your servant Purah (7:10).
and listen to what they are saying. Then your hands will be strengthened to attack the camp.” So he went with Purah his servant to the outposts where armed men were guarding the camp. (7:11).
Now the Midianites, Amalekites, and all the other people of the east had settled in the valley like a swarm of locusts, and their camels were as countless as the sand on the seashore. (7:12).

And as Gideon arrived, a man was telling his friend about a dream. “Behold, I had a dream,” he said, “and I saw a loaf of barley bread come tumbling into the Midianite camp. It struck the tent so hard that the tent overturned and collapsed.” (7:13).
His friend replied: “This is nothing less than the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite. God has delivered Midian and the whole camp into his hand.” (7:14).
When Gideon heard the dream and its interpretation, he bowed in worship. He returned to the camp of Israel and said, “Get up, for the LORD has delivered the camp of Midian into your hand.” (7:15).
And he divided the three hundred men into three companies and gave each man a ram’s horn in one hand and a large jar in the other, containing a torch. (7:16).
“Watch me and do as I do,” Gideon said. “When I come to the outskirts of the camp, do exactly as I do. (7:17).
When I and all who are with me blow our horns, then you are also to blow your horns from all around the camp and shout, ‘For the LORD and for Gideon!’” (7:18).

Gideon and the hundred men with him reached the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, just after the changing of the guard. They blew their horns and broke the jars that were in their hands. (7:19).
The three companies blew their horns and shattered their jars. Holding the torches in their left hands and the horns in their right hands, they shouted, “A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!” (7:20).
Each Israelite took his position around the camp, and the entire Midianite army fled, crying out as they ran. (7:21).

And when the three hundred rams’ horns sounded, the LORD set all the men in the camp against one another with their swords. The army fled to Beth-shittah toward Zererah as far as the border of Abel-meholah near Tabbath. (7:22).
Then the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh, and they pursued the Midianites. (7:23).

Gideon sent messengers throughout the hill country of Ephraim to say, “Come down against the Midianites and seize the waters of the Jordan ahead of them as far as Beth-barah.” So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they captured the waters of the Jordan as far as Beth-barah. (7:24).

They also captured Oreb and Zeeb, the two princes of Midian; and they killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb. So they pursued the Midianites and brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon on the other side of the Jordan. (7:25).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 20:8: The officers shall say, whoever is fearful and fainthearted, let him go back home, lest his brothers' hearts melt like his.
1 Samuel 14:6: Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few.
2 Chronicles 20:15-17: The battle is not yours but God's; take your positions, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD.
Psalm 83:9-12: Do to them as to Midian, as to Oreb and Zeeb, as to Zebah and Zalmunna at the waters of the Kishon.
Isaiah 9:4: You have broken the yoke of his burden and the rod of his oppressor, as on the day of Midian.

translationNotes.term: The spring of Harod and the hill of Moreh
translationNotes.note: Verse 1 sets the two camps. Harod is a strong spring at the foot of Mount Gilboa on the southern edge of the Jezreel valley; the hill of Moreh stands across the plain to the north, and the Midianite camp is spread between them on the valley floor. Gideon holds the high ground and looks down on the camp, which is what verse 8 and verse 12 describe, and it is what makes the night approach in verse 19 possible.

translationNotes.term: Whoever is fearful, let him return
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָרֵא וְחָרֵד (yare ve-chared), afraid and trembling
translationNotes.note: The proclamation in verse 3 is not improvised. Deuteronomy 20:8 commands an officer to say exactly this before a battle and send the fearful home so they do not melt their brothers' hearts, and 20:5 to 7 add three more exemptions: a man who has built a new house and not dedicated it, planted a vineyard and not eaten from it, or become engaged and not yet married. Twenty-two thousand take the offer, which the law had always allowed them.

translationNotes.term: A round loaf of barley bread
translationNotes.note: The dream in verse 13 is not random. Barley was the cheap grain, the food of the poor and of animals, worth roughly half of wheat by volume; 2 Kings 7:1 prices a measure of fine flour at a shekel and twice that quantity of barley at the same shekel. The whole point of the raiding described in 6:3-6 was that Midian took Israel's harvest, so a barley loaf rolling into the camp and flattening a tent is a figure the man telling it understands at once, and his friend names Gideon without being told.

Verses 16 to 20 give each of three hundred men a ram's horn in one hand and a clay jar in the other with a torch burning inside it. The jar hides the flame until it is smashed, so three hundred lights appear at once out of nothing. The horn was a unit signal, not a personal instrument; one horn spoke for a whole company, so three hundred of them sounding around a camp at the change of the middle watch told the Midianites that a very large army had them surrounded in the dark.

Verse 25 names the two Midianite princes and the two places they died, and the names match: Oreb means raven and he is killed at the rock of Oreb; Zeeb means wolf and he is killed at the winepress of Zeeb. Places took their names from what happened at them and kept them for centuries; Isaiah 10:26 still reckons on his hearers knowing the slaughter at the rock of Oreb.

stories.keyTakeaway: God reduces Gideon's army from thirty-two thousand to three hundred men, then uses this small force with trumpets and torches to rout the Midianite camp; the enemy soldiers turn on each other, and Israelite tribes pursue and kill two Midianite leaders.

stories.title: 🔥 Judges 8
summaryBullets: Then the men of Ephraim said to Gideon, “Why have you done this to us? Why did you fail to call us when you went to fight against Midian?” And they contended with him violently. (8:1).
But Gideon answered them, “Now what have I accomplished compared to you? Are not the gleanings of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer? (8:2).
God has delivered Oreb and Zeeb, the two princes of Midian, into your hand. What was I able to do compared to you?” When he had said this, their anger against him subsided. (8:3).
Then Gideon and his three hundred men came to the Jordan and crossed it, exhausted yet still in pursuit. (8:4).
So Gideon said to the men of Succoth, “Please give my troops some bread, for they are exhausted, and I am still pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian.” (8:5).
But the leaders of Succoth asked, “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession, that we should give bread to your army?” (8:6).
“Very well,” Gideon replied, “when the LORD has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will tear your flesh with the thorns and briers of the wilderness!” (8:7).
From there he went up to Penuel and asked the same from them, but the men of Penuel gave the same response as the men of Succoth. (8:8).
So Gideon told the men of Penuel, “When I return in triumph, I will tear down this tower!” (8:9).

Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their army of about fifteen thousand men — all that were left of the armies of the people of the east. A hundred and twenty thousand swordsmen had already fallen. (8:10).
And Gideon went up by way of the caravan route east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and he attacked their army, taking them by surprise. (8:11).
When Zebah and Zalmunna fled, Gideon pursued and captured these two kings of Midian, routing their entire army. (8:12).
After this, Gideon son of Joash returned from the battle along the Ascent of Heres. (8:13).
There he captured a young man of Succoth and interrogated him. The young man wrote down for him the names of the seventy-seven leaders and elders of Succoth. (8:14).

And Gideon went to the men of Succoth and said, “Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, ‘Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession, that we should give bread to your weary men?’” (8:15).
Then he took the elders of the city, and using the thorns and briers of the wilderness, he disciplined the men of Succoth. (8:16).
He also pulled down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city. (8:17).
Next, Gideon asked Zebah and Zalmunna, “What kind of men did you kill at Tabor?” “Men like you,” they answered, “each one resembling the son of a king.” (8:18).
“They were my brothers,” Gideon replied, “the sons of my mother! As surely as the LORD lives, if you had let them live, I would not kill you.” (8:19).
So he said to Jether, his firstborn, “Get up and kill them.” But the young man did not draw his sword; he was fearful because he was still a youth. (8:20).

Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, “Get up and kill us yourself, for as the man is, so is his strength.” So Gideon got up and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and he took the crescent ornaments from the necks of their camels. (8:21).
Then the Israelites said to Gideon, “Rule over us — you and your son and grandson — for you have saved us from the hand of Midian.” (8:22).
But Gideon replied, “I will not rule over you, nor will my son. The LORD shall rule over you.” (8:23).
Then he added, “Let me make a request of you, that each of you give me an earring from his plunder.” (For the enemies had gold earrings because they were Ishmaelites.) (8:24).
“We will give them gladly,” they replied. So they spread out a garment, and each man threw an earring from his plunder onto it. (8:25).

The weight of the gold earrings he had requested was 1 ,700 shekels, in addition to the crescent ornaments, the pendants, the purple garments of the kings of Midian, and the chains from the necks of their camels. (8:26).

From all this Gideon made an ephod, which he placed in Ophrah, his hometown. But soon all Israel prostituted themselves by worshiping it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his household. (8:27).
In this way Midian was subdued before the Israelites and did not raise its head again. So the land had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon, (8:28).
and he — Jerubbaal son of Joash — returned home and settled down. (8:29).
Gideon had seventy sons of his own, since he had many wives. (8:30).
His concubine, who dwelt in Shechem, also bore him a son, and he named him Abimelech. (8:31).
Later, Gideon son of Joash died at a ripe old age and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash in Ophrah of the Abiezrites. (8:32).
And as soon as Gideon was dead, the Israelites turned and prostituted themselves with the Baals, and they set up Baal-berith as their god. (8:33).
The Israelites failed to remember the LORD their God who had delivered them from the hands of all their enemies on every side. (8:34).
They did not show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) for all the good things he had done for Israel. (8:35).
crossRefs: Genesis 32:22-31: Jacob wrestles until daybreak and names the place Peniel, because he saw God face to face.
Exodus 28:6-30: The ephod of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet, with the breastpiece and the Urim and Thummim set in it.
Deuteronomy 17:14-20: The law of the king, who must not multiply wives, horses, or silver and gold for himself.
Numbers 31:1-12: Israel's earlier war on Midian, in which the five kings of Midian are killed.
Judges 9:1-6: Abimelech, the son born at Shechem, kills his seventy brothers on one stone and is made king there.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֹלֵלוֹת (olelot), gleanings of the vineyard
translationNotes.note: Gideon answers an armed complaint with a vine-grower's proverb in verse 2. The olelot are the small clusters left on the vines after the main picking, which the law reserved for the poor and the foreigner and forbade the owner to go back for (Leviticus 19:9-10, Deuteronomy 24:21). He is saying that Ephraim's leftovers beat his own whole harvest, and verse 3 says the flattery worked.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֻכּוֹת (Sukkot), booths - פְּנוּאֵל (Penuel), the face of God
translationNotes.note: Both towns stand on the Jabbok in the Jordan valley east of the river, and Jacob named both of them: Peniel where he wrestled through the night and said he had seen God face to face, and Succoth where he built shelters for his livestock (Genesis 32:30, 33:17). They refuse bread to three hundred exhausted men because they expect Gideon to lose and do not want Midianite reprisals afterwards. Verses 16 and 17 record what he does to them on the way back.

Verses 21 and 26 have Gideon strip crescent-shaped pendants from the necks of the kings' camels, along with chains and pendants. Saharon means little moon, and the crescent was one of the commonest ornaments and amulets in that world, worn by people and hung on valuable animals. Isaiah 3:18 lists the same item among the finery stripped from the women of Jerusalem.

Verse 26 weighs the earrings alone at 1,700 shekels. A shekel is a weight, not a coin, about two-fifths of an ounce, so this is roughly forty-three pounds of gold, and it does not count the crescents, pendants, purple garments and camel chains listed with it. The purple is worth noting on its own: that dye came from a sea snail harvested on the Phoenician coast and was among the most costly substances anyone traded in.

The ephod of the law is a garment, not an image: a sleeveless vestment of gold, blue, purple and scarlet worn by the high priest over his robe, with two shoulder pieces and a woven band, and the breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim fastened to the front of it (Exodus 28:6-30). Because the means of enquiring of God hung on it, bring the ephod came to mean ask God a question (1 Samuel 23:9-12). Verse 27 has Gideon make one out of forty-three pounds of captured gold and set it up in his home town, and Israel prostitutes itself to it there.

stories.keyTakeaway: Gideon appeases angry Ephraimites, pursues and defeats the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, and punishes Sukkoth and Peniel for refusing aid; he refuses kingship but collects gold that becomes an idol in Ophrah. After Gideon dies, Israel abandons the LORD and forgets his deliverance.

stories.title: 🔥 Judges 9
summaryBullets: Now Abimelech son of Jerubbaal went to his mother’s brothers at Shechem and said to them and to all the clan of his mother, (9:1).
“Please ask all the leaders of Shechem, ‘Is it better for you that seventy men, all the sons of Jerubbaal, rule over you, or just one man?’ Remember that I am your own flesh and blood.” (9:2).

And when his mother’s brothers spoke all these words about him in the presence of all the leaders of Shechem, their hearts were inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, “He is our brother.” (9:3).
So they gave him seventy shekels of silver from the temple of Baal-berith, with which Abimelech hired some worthless and reckless men to follow him. (9:4).
He went to his father’s house in Ophrah, and on one stone murdered his seventy brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal. But Jotham, the youngest son of Jerubbaal, survived, because he hid himself. (9:5).
Then all the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo gathered beside the oak at the pillar in Shechem and proceeded to make Abimelech their king. (9:6).
When this was reported to Jotham, he climbed to the top of Mount Gerizim, raised his voice, and cried out: “Listen to me, O leaders of Shechem, and may God listen to you. (9:7).
One day the trees set out to anoint a king for themselves. They said to the olive tree, ‘Reign over us.’ (9:8).
But the olive tree replied, ‘Should I stop giving my oil that honors both God and man, to hold sway over the trees?’ (9:9).
Then the trees said to the fig tree, ‘Come and reign over us.’ (9:10).
But the fig tree replied, ‘Should I stop giving my sweetness and my good fruit, to hold sway over the trees?’ (9:11).
Then the trees said to the grapevine, ‘Come and reign over us.’ (9:12).
But the grapevine replied, ‘Should I stop giving my wine that cheers both God and man, to hold sway over the trees?’ (9:13).
Finally all the trees said to the thornbush, ‘Come and reign over us.’ (9:14).

But the thornbush replied, ‘If you really are anointing me as king over you, come and find refuge in my shade. But if not, may fire come out of the thornbush and consume the cedars of Lebanon.’ (9:15).
Now if you have acted faithfully and honestly in making Abimelech king, if you have done well by Jerubbaal and his family, and if you have done to him as he deserves— (9:16).
for my father fought for you and risked his life to deliver you from the hand of Midian, (9:17).

but you have risen up against my father’s house this day and killed his seventy sons on a single stone, and you have made Abimelech, the son of his maidservant, king over the leaders of Shechem because he is your brother — (9:18).
if you have acted faithfully and honestly toward Jerubbaal and his house this day, then may you rejoice in Abimelech, and he in you. (9:19).
But if not, may fire come from Abimelech and consume the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo, and may fire come from the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo and consume Abimelech.” (9:20).
Then Jotham ran away, escaping to Beer, and he lived there for fear of his brother Abimelech. (9:21).
After Abimelech had reigned over Israel for three years, (9:22).
God sent a spirit of animosity between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem and caused them to treat Abimelech deceitfully, (9:23).

in order that the crime against the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come to justice and their blood be avenged on their brother Abimelech and on the leaders of Shechem, who had helped him murder his brothers. (9:24).
The leaders of Shechem set up an ambush against Abimelech on the hilltops, and they robbed all who passed by them on the road. So this was reported to Abimelech. (9:25).
Meanwhile, Gaal son of Ebed came with his brothers and crossed into Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem put their confidence in him. (9:26).

And after they had gone out into the fields, gathered grapes from their vineyards, and trodden them, they held a festival and went into the house of their god; and as they ate and drank, they cursed Abimelech. (9:27).

Then Gaal son of Ebed said, “Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his officer? You are to serve the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem. Why should we serve Abimelech? (9:28).
If only this people were under my authority, I would remove Abimelech; I would say to him, ‘Muster your army and come out!’” (9:29).
When Zebul the governor of the city heard the words of Gaal son of Ebed, he burned with anger. (9:30).
So he covertly sent messengers to Abimelech to say, “Look, Gaal son of Ebed and his brothers have come to Shechem and are stirring up the city against you. (9:31).
Now then, tonight you and the people with you are to come and lie in wait in the fields. (9:32).
And in the morning at sunrise, get up and advance against the city. When Gaal and his men come out against you, do to them whatever you are able.” (9:33).
So Abimelech and all his troops set out by night and lay in wait against Shechem in four companies. (9:34).
Now Gaal son of Ebed went out and stood at the entrance of the city gate just as Abimelech and his men came out from their hiding places. (9:35).
When Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, “Look, people are coming down from the mountains!” But Zebul replied, “The shadows of the mountains look like men to you.” (9:36).
Then Gaal spoke up again, “Look, people are coming down from the center of the land, and one company is coming by way of the Diviners’ Oak.” (9:37).
“Where is your gloating now?” Zebul replied. “You said, ‘Who is Abimelech that we should serve him?’ Are these not the people you ridiculed? Go out now and fight them!” (9:38).
So Gaal went out before the leaders of Shechem and fought against Abimelech, (9:39).
but Abimelech pursued him, and Gaal fled before him. And many Shechemites fell wounded all the way to the entrance of the gate. (9:40).
Abimelech stayed in Arumah, and Zebul drove Gaal and his brothers out of Shechem. (9:41).
The next day the people of Shechem went out into the fields, and this was reported to Abimelech. (9:42).
So he took his men, divided them into three companies, and lay in wait in the fields. When he saw the people coming out of the city, he rose up against them and attacked them. (9:43).

Then Abimelech and the companies with him rushed forward and took their stand at the entrance of the city gate. The other two companies rushed against all who were in the fields and struck them down. (9:44).
And all that day Abimelech fought against the city until he had captured it and killed its people. Then he demolished the city and sowed it with salt. (9:45).
On hearing of this, all the leaders in the tower of Shechem entered the inner chamber of the temple of El-berith. (9:46).
And when Abimelech was told that all the leaders in the tower of Shechem were gathered there, (9:47).

he and all his men went up to Mount Zalmon. Abimelech took his axe in his hand and cut a branch from the trees, which he lifted to his shoulder, saying to his men, “Hurry and do what you have seen me do.” (9:48).

So each man also cut his own branch and followed Abimelech. Then they piled the branches against the inner chamber and set it on fire above them, killing everyone in the tower of Shechem, about a thousand men and women. (9:49).
Then Abimelech went to Thebez, encamped against it, and captured it. (9:50).
But there was a strong tower inside the city, and all the men, women, and leaders of the city fled there. They locked themselves in and went up to the roof of the tower. (9:51).
When Abimelech came to attack the tower, he approached its entrance to set it on fire. (9:52).
But a woman dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech’s head, crushing his skull. (9:53).
He quickly called his armor-bearer, saying, “Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’” So Abimelech’s armor-bearer ran his sword through him, and he died. (9:54).
And when the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, they all went home. (9:55).
In this way God repaid the wickedness that Abimelech had done to his father in murdering his seventy brothers. (9:56).
And God also brought all the wickedness of the men of Shechem back upon their own heads. So the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came upon them. (9:57).
crossRefs: Judges 8:29-32: Gideon's seventy sons, and the son born to his concubine at Shechem, whom he named Abimelech.
Deuteronomy 11:29: Set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal.
Joshua 24:25-27: Joshua makes a covenant at Shechem and sets a great stone under the oak by the sanctuary of the LORD.
2 Samuel 11:21: Joab's messenger is told to mention Abimelech, killed when a woman dropped a millstone on him from the wall.
Judges 8:33-35: After Gideon dies Israel makes Baal-berith their god and shows no loyalty to Gideon's house.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲבִימֶלֶךְ (Abimelek), my father is king
translationNotes.note: Verse 5 is a dynastic massacre: every rival claimant killed together, on one stone, in one act. Abimelech's own name means my father is king, which is what Gideon had refused to be (8:23), and his claim rests on his mother's family at Shechem rather than his father's house at Ophrah. Jehu does the same thing to Ahab's seventy sons at Samaria, and has their heads sent to him in baskets (2 Kings 10:1-8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּעַל בְּרִית (Baal-berit), lord of the covenant - אֵל בְּרִית (El-berit), god of the covenant
translationNotes.note: The god of Shechem, named at 8:33 and here in verses 4 and 46, where the same shrine is called the temple of El-berith. Two details show what such a temple was for besides worship: verse 4 has Abimelech drawn seventy shekels of silver out of its treasury to hire men, so it held the town's money, and verse 46 has the townspeople take refuge in its stronghold, so it was also the strongest building they had. Shechem is the town where Joshua had made Israel swear its covenant to the LORD (Joshua 24:25).

The fable in verses 8 to 15 is built out of the four plants everyone listening farmed. The olive, the fig and the vine were the crops a hill farm lived on, slow to grow, worth years of care, and all three are made to say they will not leave their own work to sway over the trees. The atad is a scrubby thorn that gives no fruit and no shade and burns fiercely once alight, which is why the last line of the fable is about fire coming out of it.

Shechem sits in the pass between two mountains: Gerizim on the south, about 2,890 feet, and Ebal on the north, about 3,084 feet. Moses assigned the blessings to Gerizim and the curses to Ebal, and Joshua read the whole law between them (Deuteronomy 11:29, Joshua 8:30-35). Jotham climbs the blessing mountain in verse 7 and shouts a curse down into the pass.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פֶּלַח רֶכֶב (pelah rekhev), the rider stone
translationNotes.note: Household grain was ground between two stones, a fixed lower one and a shaped upper one that a woman worked back and forth with both hands. It is a solid block of basalt, and dropped from a tower it is a killing weight. Verse 53 is remembered well enough that Joab quotes it as a caution about approaching walls generations later (2 Samuel 11:21).

stories.keyTakeaway: Abimelek murders his seventy brothers to become king of Shechem; Jotham, the sole survivor, pronounces a curse on both Abimelek and the city. After three years, conflict erupts between Abimelek and Shechem; Abimelek destroys the city and its tower, then dies when a woman drops a millstone on his head at Thebez.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judges 10
summaryBullets: After the time of Abimelech, a man of Issachar, Tola son of Puah, the son of Dodo, rose up to save Israel. He lived in Shamir, in the hill country of Ephraim. (10:1).
Tola judged Israel twenty-three years, and when he died, he was buried in Shamir. (10:2).
Tola was followed by Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years. (10:3).
He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys. And they had thirty towns in the land of Gilead, which to this day are called Havvoth-jair. (10:4).
When Jair died, he was buried in Kamon. (10:5).

And again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD. They served the Baals, the Ashtoreths, the gods of Aram, Sidon, and Moab, and the gods of the Ammonites and Philistines. Thus they forsook the LORD and did not serve Him. (10:6).
So the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He sold them into the hands of the Philistines and Ammonites, (10:7).
who that very year harassed and oppressed the Israelites, and they did so for eighteen years to all the Israelites on the other side of the Jordan in Gilead, the land of the Amorites. (10:8).
The Ammonites also crossed the Jordan to fight against Judah, Benjamin, and the house of Ephraim, and Israel was in deep distress. (10:9).
Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD, saying, “We have sinned against You, for we have indeed forsaken our God and served the Baals.” (10:10).
The LORD replied, “When the Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, Philistines, (10:11).
Sidonians, Amalekites, and Maonites oppressed you and you cried out to Me, did I not save you from their hands? (10:12).
But you have forsaken Me and served other gods, so I will no longer save you. (10:13).
Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen. Let them save you in your time of trouble.” (10:14).
“We have sinned,” the Israelites said to the LORD. “Deal with us as You see fit; but please deliver us today!” (10:15).
So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and He could no longer bear the misery of Israel. (10:16).
Then the Ammonites were called to arms and camped in Gilead, and the Israelites assembled and camped at Mizpah. (10:17).
And the rulers of Gilead said to one another, “Whoever will launch the attack against the Ammonites will be the head of all who live in Gilead.” (10:18).
crossRefs: Judges 2:11-19: The repeating pattern of forsaking the LORD, being sold to enemies, crying out, and a judge raised up.
Deuteronomy 32:37-38: Where are their gods, the rock in which they took refuge? Let them rise up and help you.
1 Samuel 12:10: We have sinned, for we have forsaken the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth.
Genesis 19:36-38: Lot's two daughters bear Moab and Ben-ammi, the fathers of Moab and Ammon.
Jeremiah 2:28: Where are your gods that you made for yourself? As many as your cities are your gods, O Judah.

translationNotes.note: Ammon descended from Lot through his younger daughter, which is what Genesis 19:38 records, so Israel and Ammon were reckoned distant kin. Their country lay east of the Jordan on the desert edge, with its capital at Rabbah, the site of modern Amman, and their god was Milcom, also called Molech, whose worship took children in fire (1 Kings 11:5-7, 2 Kings 23:10). Verses 7 to 9 have them cross the river and press Gilead for eighteen years.

Verse 17 gathers Israel at Mizpah, and the name means lookout or watchpost, from the verb to keep watch. This is the Gileadite Mizpah east of the Jordan, where Jephthah is made head in 11:11 and where he comes home in 11:34, and it is not the Mizpah in Benjamin where Samuel later gathers the nation (1 Samuel 7:5-6). Genesis 31:49 attaches the same name to the heap of stones Jacob and Laban set up as a boundary, for the reason that the LORD would watch between them.

Verse 6 lists them one by one: the Baals and the Ashtaroth of Canaan, the gods of Aram, of Sidon, of Moab, of Ammon, and of the Philistines. Each name is a real cult with its own rites. Baal was the storm god who was believed to give rain, Ashtoreth the goddess served with sexual rites, Chemosh of Moab and Milcom of Ammon both took children in fire, and Dagon of the Philistines was a god of grain. Israel is not described as vaguely drifting; it is described taking up all of them.

The highland east of the Jordan between the Yarmuk and the Arnon, wooded, well watered, and good for flocks; it was known for balm (Jeremiah 8:22). Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh settled there, which left them outside the Jordan and first in line when Ammon pushed west. Verse 8 has the Ammonite pressure crush Gilead for eighteen years before it crosses the river.

stories.keyTakeaway: Tola and Jair each judge Israel for two decades before the people turn to foreign gods, prompting God to let the Philistines and Ammonites oppress them for eighteen years; after Israel repents and removes idols, the Ammonites gather for war and the Gileadites assemble at Mizpah, promising leadership to whoever attacks first.

headings.text: Oppression by the Philistines and Ammonites

stories.title: ⚔️ Judges 11
summaryBullets: Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of valor; he was the son of a prostitute, and Gilead was his father. (11:1).
And Gilead’s wife bore him sons who grew up, drove Jephthah out, and said to him, “You shall have no inheritance in our father’s house, because you are the son of another woman.” (11:2).
So Jephthah fled from his brothers and settled in the land of Tob, where worthless men gathered around him and traveled with him. (11:3).
Some time later, when the Ammonites fought against Israel (11:4).
and made war with them, the elders of Gilead went to get Jephthah from the land of Tob. (11:5).
“Come,” they said, “be our commander, so that we can fight against the Ammonites.” (11:6).
Jephthah replied to the elders of Gilead, “Did you not hate me and expel me from my father’s house? Why then have you come to me now, when you are in distress?” (11:7).
They answered Jephthah, “This is why we now turn to you, that you may go with us, fight the Ammonites, and become leader over all of us who live in Gilead.” (11:8).
