But Jephthah asked them, “If you take me back to fight the Ammonites and the LORD gives them to me, will I really be your leader?” (11:9).
And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “The LORD is our witness if we do not do as you say.” (11:10).
So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him their leader and commander. And Jephthah repeated all his terms in the presence of the LORD at Mizpah. (11:11).
Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites, saying, “What do you have against me that you have come to fight against my land?” (11:12).

The king of the Ammonites answered Jephthah’s messengers, “When Israel came up out of Egypt, they seized my land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and all the way to the Jordan. Now, therefore, restore it peaceably.” (11:13).
Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites (11:14).
to tell him, “This is what Jephthah says: Israel did not take away the land of Moab or of the Ammonites. (11:15).
But when Israel came up out of Egypt, they traveled through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh. (11:16).

Then Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, ‘Please let us pass through your land,’ but the king of Edom would not listen. They also sent messengers to the king of Moab, but he would not consent. So Israel stayed in Kadesh. (11:17).

Then Israel traveled through the wilderness and bypassed the lands of Edom and Moab. They came to the east side of the land of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon. But they did not enter the territory of Moab, since the Arnon was its border. (11:18).
And Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled in Heshbon, and said to him, ‘Please let us pass through your land into our own place.’ (11:19).
But Sihon would not trust Israel to pass through his territory. So he gathered all his people, encamped in Jahaz, and fought with Israel. (11:20).

Then the LORD, the God of Israel, delivered Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, who defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites who inhabited that country, (11:21).
seizing all the land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan. (11:22).
Now since the LORD, the God of Israel, has driven out the Amorites from before His people Israel, should you now possess it? (11:23).
Do you not possess whatever your god Chemosh grants you? So also, we possess whatever the LORD our God has granted us. (11:24).
Are you now so much better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever contend with Israel or fight against them? (11:25).
For three hundred years Israel has lived in Heshbon, Aroer, and their villages, as well as all the cities along the banks of the Arnon. Why did you not take them back during that time? (11:26).
I have not sinned against you, but you have done me wrong by waging war against me. May the LORD, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites.” (11:27).
But the king of the Ammonites paid no heed to the message Jephthah sent him. (11:28).
Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, then through Mizpah of Gilead. And from there he advanced against the Ammonites. (11:29).
Jephthah made this vow to the LORD: “If indeed You will deliver the Ammonites into my hand, (11:30).
then whatever comes out the door of my house to greet me on my triumphant return from the Ammonites will belong to the LORD, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering.” (11:31).
So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the LORD delivered them into his hand. (11:32).
With a great blow he devastated twenty cities from Aroer to the vicinity of Minnith, as far as Abel-keramim. So the Ammonites were subdued before the Israelites. (11:33).
And when Jephthah returned home to Mizpah, there was his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing! She was his only child; he had no son or daughter besides her. (11:34).

As soon as Jephthah saw her, he tore his clothes and said, “No! Not my daughter! You have brought me to my knees! You have brought great misery upon me, for I have given my word to the LORD and cannot take it back.” (11:35).
“My father,” she replied, “you have given your word to the LORD. Do to me as you have said, for the LORD has avenged you of your enemies, the Ammonites.” (11:36).
She also said to her father, “Let me do this one thing: Let me wander for two months through the mountains with my friends and mourn my virginity.” (11:37).
“Go,” he said. And he sent her away for two months. So she left with her friends and mourned her virginity upon the mountains. (11:38).
After two months, she returned to her father, and he did to her as he had vowed. And she had never had relations with a man. So it has become a custom in Israel (11:39).
that each year the young women of Israel go out for four days to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite. (11:40).
crossRefs: Numbers 21:21-31: Israel asks Sihon for passage, is refused and attacked, and takes his land, the history Jephthah recites.
Deuteronomy 2:19: Do not harass the sons of Ammon or contend with them, for I have given their land to the sons of Lot.
Leviticus 27:1-8: The scale of silver payments for redeeming a person who has been vowed to the LORD.
Deuteronomy 12:31: They burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods, which the LORD hates.
Genesis 22:1-14: Abraham is stopped before he strikes, and a ram caught in the thicket is offered instead.

translationNotes.note: A neder is a promise made to God, usually offering something in return for help, and the law treats it as absolutely binding once spoken: Numbers 30:2 says a man shall not break his word, Deuteronomy 23:21-23 says it is no sin not to vow but delay in paying is charged against you, and Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 repeats it. The law also provided a way out that Jephthah does not take. Leviticus 27:1-8 sets a fixed scale of silver by which a person vowed to the LORD is redeemed instead of given: fifty shekels for a man between twenty and sixty, thirty for a woman, ten for a girl between five and twenty, with reduced rates for the very young and the old.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה (ishah zonah), a prostitute
translationNotes.note: Verses 1 to 3 turn on inheritance law. Jephthah is Gilead's son by a prostitute, and his half-brothers by the wife expel him with the words you shall have no inheritance in our father's house. Land passed to the sons of the household, and a son with no standing in it had nothing to hold and nowhere to go, so he leaves for Tob, north-east of Gilead, and worthless men gather to him. The same elders who let that happen come looking for him to command their army in verse 6.

Verse 24 has Jephthah name Chemosh in his message about disputed land. Chemosh was the national god of Moab; Numbers 21:29 calls the Moabites the people of Chemosh, Solomon built him a high place east of Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7), and 2 Kings 3:27 records a king of Moab burning his own heir on the wall. King Mesha's inscription, found at Dhiban in 1868, credits Chemosh with his victories over Israel in his own words.

Verses 39 and 40 close with a yearly practice: the daughters of Israel went out four days every year on account of Jephthah's daughter. Israel kept the memory of what a vow cost by setting aside a fixed period for it, the same way the nation kept fasts and feasts. The book records the custom without excusing the vow that caused it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Gilead’s elders recall Jephthah, the outcast son of a prostitute, to command them against Ammon, and he answers the Ammonite king’s land claim by recounting how the LORD gave Israel the land of Sihon. He vows to offer up whatever first comes out of his house if the LORD grants victory; the LORD delivers Ammon and his only daughter comes out to meet him, and after two months mourning her virginity he does to her as he vowed, so Israel’s daughters go out each year to lament her.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judges 12
summaryBullets: Then the men of Ephraim assembled and crossed the Jordan to Zaphon. They said to Jephthah, “Why have you crossed over to fight the Ammonites without calling us to go with you? We will burn your house down with you inside!” (12:1).
But Jephthah replied, “My people and I had a serious conflict with the Ammonites, and when I called, you did not save me out of their hands. (12:2).
When I saw that you would not save me, I risked my life and crossed over to the Ammonites, and the LORD delivered them into my hand. Why then have you come today to fight against me?” (12:3).

Jephthah then gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim. And the men of Gilead struck them down because the Ephraimites had said, “You Gileadites are fugitives in Ephraim, living in the territories of Ephraim and Manasseh.” (12:4).

The Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan leading to Ephraim, and whenever a fugitive from Ephraim would say, “Let me cross over,” the Gileadites would ask him, “Are you an Ephraimite?” If he answered, “No,” (12:5).

they told him, “Please say Shibboleth.” If he said, “Sibboleth,” because he could not pronounce it correctly, they seized him and killed him at the fords of the Jordan. So at that time 42,000 Ephraimites were killed. (12:6).
Jephthah judged Israel six years, and when he died, he was buried in one of the cities of Gilead. (12:7).
After Jephthah, Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel. (12:8).

He had thirty sons, as well as thirty daughters whom he gave in marriage to men outside his clan; and for his sons he brought back thirty wives from elsewhere. Ibzan judged Israel seven years. (12:9).
Then Ibzan died, and he was buried in Bethlehem. (12:10).
After Ibzan, Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel ten years. (12:11).
Then Elon the Zebulunite died, and he was buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun. (12:12).
After Elon, Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, judged Israel. (12:13).
He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys. And he judged Israel eight years. (12:14).
Then Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, died, and he was buried at Pirathon in Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites. (12:15).
crossRefs: Judges 8:1-3: Ephraim quarrels with Gideon in the same terms for not being called to the fight, and he answers them softly.
Proverbs 15:1: A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
Joshua 22:10-34: The eastern tribes build an altar by the Jordan and the rest of Israel nearly goes to war over it.
Judges 3:28: Ehud seizes the fords of the Jordan against Moab and lets no one cross over.
Nehemiah 13:23-24: Half the children of the mixed marriages spoke the language of Ashdod and could not speak the language of Judah.

translationNotes.note: The word itself means an ear of grain, or in other passages a flowing stream, and its meaning is beside the point; it was chosen because it starts with the sh sound that the Ephraimite dialect across the river did not use. A man could claim any tribe he liked, but he could not change how his mouth had been trained to speak since childhood. Verse 6 records the toll: forty-two thousand Ephraimites killed at the crossings, on the evidence of one syllable.

The Jordan runs in a deep, thicketed trench and can only be crossed at a handful of shallow places. Whoever holds the fords controls who gets across, which is why they are seized three separate times in this book (Judges 3:28, 7:24, and here in verse 5). An army cut off from the fords is trapped on the wrong side of the river with nowhere to go.

translationNotes.term: Thirty daughters married outside the clan
translationNotes.note: Verse 9 says Ibzan sent thirty daughters out of his clan in marriage and brought thirty wives in from outside for his sons. Marriage was a treaty between households, and daughters going out and wives coming in built a network of obligation across a whole region. Sixty such matches is a record of a man who ruled by alliance, which is why the writer counts them the way he counts years in office.

Verse 14 counts Abdon's forty sons and thirty grandsons riding seventy donkeys, and 10:4 does the same for Jair's thirty sons. This is a note about standing, not transport: before horses were common in Israel the donkey was the mount of a man of rank, and a household that could put seventy men on their own animals was wealthy and settled. Zechariah 9:9 draws on the same picture of a king coming on a donkey.

stories.keyTakeaway: Ephraim confronts Jephthah over not being called to fight the Ammonites; Jephthah defeats them at the Jordan, using the word "Shibboleth" to identify and kill forty-two thousand Ephraimites. Jephthah leads Israel six years before dying, followed by judges Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon.

stories.title: 🦁 Judges 13
summaryBullets: Again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD, so He delivered them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years. (13:1).
Now there was a man from Zorah named Manoah, from the clan of the Danites, whose wife was barren and had no children. (13:2).
The angel of the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, “It is true that you are barren and have no children; but you will conceive and give birth to a son. (13:3).
Now please be careful not to drink wine or strong drink, and not to eat anything unclean. (13:4).

For behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son. And no razor shall touch his head, because the boy will be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he will begin the deliverance of Israel from the hand of the Philistines.” (13:5).

So the woman went and told her husband, “A man of God came to me. His appearance was like the angel of God, exceedingly awesome. I did not ask him where he came from, and he did not tell me his name. (13:6).

But he said to me, ‘Behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son. Now, therefore, do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean, because the boy will be a Nazirite to God from the womb until the day of his death.’” (13:7).
Then Manoah prayed to the LORD, “Please, O Lord, let the man of God You sent us come to us again to teach us how to raise the boy who is to be born.” (13:8).
And God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel of God returned to the woman as she was sitting in the field; but her husband Manoah was not with her. (13:9).
The woman ran quickly to tell her husband, “Behold, the man who came to me the other day has reappeared!” (13:10).
So Manoah got up and followed his wife. When he came to the man, he asked, “Are you the man who spoke to my wife?” “I am, ” he said. (13:11).
Then Manoah asked, “When your words come to pass, what will be the boy’s rule of life and mission?” (13:12).
So the angel of the LORD answered Manoah, “Your wife is to do everything I told her. (13:13).
She must not eat anything that comes from the vine, nor drink any wine or strong drink, nor eat anything unclean. She must do everything I have commanded her.” (13:14).
“Please stay here,” Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, “and we will prepare a young goat for you.” (13:15).

And the angel of the LORD replied, “Even if I stay, I will not eat your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD.” For Manoah did not know that it was the angel of the LORD. (13:16).
Then Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, “What is your name, so that we may honor you when your word comes to pass?” (13:17).
“Why do you ask my name,” said the angel of the LORD, “since it is beyond comprehension?” (13:18).
Then Manoah took a young goat and a grain offering and offered them on a rock to the LORD. And as Manoah and his wife looked on, the LORD did a marvelous thing. (13:19).
When the flame went up from the altar to the sky, the angel of the LORD ascended in the flame. When Manoah and his wife saw this, they fell facedown to the ground. (13:20).
And when the angel of the LORD did not appear again to Manoah and his wife, Manoah realized that it had been the angel of the LORD. (13:21).
“We are going to die,” he said to his wife, “for we have seen God!” (13:22).

But his wife replied, “If the LORD had intended to kill us, He would not have accepted the burnt offering and the grain offering from our hands, nor would He have shown us all these things or spoken to us this way.” (13:23).
So the woman gave birth to a son and named him Samson. The boy grew, and the LORD blessed him. (13:24).
And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him at Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol. (13:25).
crossRefs: Numbers 6:1-21: The law of the Nazirite vow: nothing from the vine, no razor on the head, no contact with a dead body.
1 Samuel 1:11: Hannah vows that if the LORD gives her a son, no razor will ever touch his head.
Genesis 18:9-15: Sarah is promised a son in her old age and laughs to herself behind the tent door.
Exodus 33:20: You cannot see My face, for man shall not see Me and live.
Luke 1:11-17: An angel promises Zechariah a son who will drink no wine or strong drink and will be filled with the Spirit from birth.

translationNotes.term: A Nazirite to God from the womb
translationNotes.note: From nazar, to separate. Numbers 6:1-21 sets out the vow in full: nothing at all from the grapevine, not wine, not vinegar, not fresh or dried grapes, not even the skins or the seeds; no razor on the head for the whole term; and no going near a dead body, not even a father's or mother's. It was normally taken for a set period and ended at the sanctuary with offerings and the shaving of the head, the hair burned under the fellowship sacrifice. Samson's is imposed for life and begins before he is born.

Zorah and Eshtaol are villages in the Sorek valley on the western edge of the hill country, looking straight out onto Philistine territory, which is why this family lives under Philistine rule. Mahaneh-dan means camp of Dan and lies between the two. Dan never took the coastal allotment it was given, because the Amorites forced the tribe back up into the hills (Judges 1:34), and Judges 18:11-12 has six hundred armed Danites camping at this same spot on their way north to take Laish instead.

Malakh means one who is sent, a messenger, and the word is used of human couriers as readily as of heavenly ones. Manoah's wife first reports him as a man of God, the ordinary term for a prophet, and Manoah only draws his conclusion after the figure goes up in the altar flame. His reaction in verse 22, that they will die because they have seen God, rests on the rule stated in Exodus 33:20 and on Jacob's surprise in Genesis 32:30 at surviving the encounter.

translationNotes.term: Why do you ask my name
translationNotes.note: The word rendered beyond comprehension is peli, from pala, to be wonderful or out of reach. The chapter then uses the same root twice more: verse 19 says the LORD acted wondrously, maphli laasot, while Manoah and his wife watched. The same root supplies the first title in Isaiah 9:6, pele yoets, Wonderful Counsellor. The answer and the sign are the same word.

translationNotes.term: A burnt offering and a grain offering on a rock
translationNotes.note: An olah is the whole burnt offering, the one sacrifice burned entirely with no portion eaten by priest or worshipper; the name means that which goes up. A minchah is a grain offering of flour and oil. Manoah uses a bare rock rather than a built altar, exactly as Gideon did when the angel touched the meat and bread with his staff and fire came up out of the rock (Judges 6:19-21).

stories.keyTakeaway: An angel of the LORD appears to Manoah's barren wife, promising her a son who will be a Nazirite dedicated to delivering Israel from the Philistines; when Manoah offers a sacrifice, the angel ascends in the flame and the woman gives birth to Samson.

stories.title: 🦁 Judges 14
summaryBullets: One day Samson went down to Timnah, where he saw a young Philistine woman. (14:1).
So he returned and told his father and mother, “I have seen a daughter of the Philistines in Timnah. Now get her for me as a wife.” (14:2).

But his father and mother replied, “Can’t you find a young woman among your relatives or among any of our people? Must you go to the uncircumcised Philistines to get a wife?” But Samson told his father, “Get her for me, for she is pleasing to my eyes.” (14:3).
(Now his father and mother did not know this was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion to move against the Philistines; for at that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel.) (14:4).
Then Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother and came to the vineyards of Timnah. Suddenly a young lion came roaring at him, (14:5).
and the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him, and he tore the lion apart with his bare hands as one would tear a young goat. But he did not tell his father or mother what he had done. (14:6).
Then Samson continued on his way down and spoke to the woman, because she was pleasing to his eyes. (14:7).
When Samson returned later to take her, he left the road to see the lion’s carcass, and in it was a swarm of bees, along with their honey. (14:8).

So he scooped some honey into his hands and ate it as he went along. And when he returned to his father and mother, he gave some to them and they ate it. But he did not tell them that he had taken the honey from the lion’s carcass. (14:9).
Then his father went to visit the woman, and Samson prepared a feast there, as was customary for the bridegroom. (14:10).
And when the Philistines saw him, they selected thirty men to accompany him. (14:11).
“Let me tell you a riddle,” Samson said to them. “If you can solve it for me within the seven days of the feast, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes. (14:12).
But if you cannot solve it, you must give me thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes.” “Tell us your riddle,” they replied. “Let us hear it.” (14:13).
So he said to them: “Out of the eater came something to eat, and out of the strong came something sweet.” For three days they were unable to explain the riddle. (14:14).

So on the fourth day they said to Samson’s wife, “Entice your husband to explain the riddle to us, or we will burn you and your father’s household to death. Did you invite us here to rob us?” (14:15).

Then Samson’s wife came to him, weeping, and said, “You hate me! You do not really love me! You have posed to my people a riddle, but have not explained it to me.” “Look,” he said, “I have not even explained it to my father or mother, so why should I explain it to you?” (14:16).
She wept the whole seven days of the feast, and finally on the seventh day, because she had pressed him so much, he told her the answer. And in turn she explained the riddle to her people. (14:17).

Before sunset on the seventh day, the men of the city said to Samson: “What is sweeter than honey? And what is stronger than a lion?” So he said to them: “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have solved my riddle!” (14:18).

Then the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon, killed thirty of their men, took their apparel, and gave their clothes to those who had solved the riddle. And burning with anger, Samson returned to his father’s house, (14:19).
and his wife was given to one of the men who had accompanied him. (14:20).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 7:3-4: Do not intermarry with them, for they will turn your children away from following Me to serve other gods.
Numbers 6:6-8: A Nazirite shall not go near a dead body all the days of his separation to the LORD.
Leviticus 11:27,39: Whoever touches the carcass of an unclean animal is unclean until the evening.
Judges 3:1-4: The Philistines were left in the land to test Israel and to teach war to those who had not known it.
Genesis 29:27: Complete the week of this one, the seven-day wedding feast behind the seven days of the riddle.

translationNotes.note: A chidah is a saying deliberately built to be hard, and posing them was a contest of wit, not a children's game; the queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon with them (1 Kings 10:1), and Proverbs 1:6 lists them among the things wisdom teaches a man to read. Samson's, in verse 14, cannot be solved by thinking, because it describes a private incident nobody else saw. The stake in verses 12 and 13 is thirty linen wraps and thirty changes of clothing, a serious wager for thirty village men.

translationNotes.term: The lion's carcass and the Nazirite rule
translationNotes.note: Verses 8 and 9 have Samson turn aside to the dead lion, scoop honey out of it with his hands, eat it as he walks, and give some to his parents without telling them where it came from. Numbers 6:6-7 forbids a Nazirite to go near any dead body at all, even a father's or mother's, and touching a carcass makes any Israelite unclean (Leviticus 11:24-28). The chapter reports his silence about it, and expects the reader to know what has been broken.

Verse 1 has Samson go down to Timnah, a Philistine town in the Sorek valley a few miles down from his home at Zorah; down is literal, since it is a drop from the hill country toward the coastal plain. It had been allotted to Judah and then to Dan (Joshua 15:10, 19:43) and neither held it. Deuteronomy 7:3 forbids marriage with the peoples of the land, which is exactly what his parents say to him in verse 3.

A wedding was not a ceremony but a week of eating and drinking at the bride's town, with the groom's side hosting and thirty local men attached to him as companions (verse 11). Jacob's week for Leah works the same way (Genesis 29:27). The riddle and its wager in verses 12 and 13 are entertainment for the feast, thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes being a substantial stake.

stories.keyTakeaway: Samson sees a Philistine woman in Timnah, insists on marrying her despite his parents' objections, and tears apart a lion with his bare hands on the way there. At his wedding feast he poses a riddle to thirty Philistine men, but when his wife coerces him into revealing the answer, the Spirit of the LORD empowers him to kill thirty men in Ashkelon and give their clothes to the riddle solvers; his wife is then given to another man.

stories.title: 🦁 Judges 15
summaryBullets: Later on, at the time of the wheat harvest, Samson took a young goat and went to visit his wife. “I want to go to my wife in her room,” he said. But her father would not let him enter. (15:1).
“I was sure that you thoroughly hated her,” said her father, “so I gave her to one of the men who accompanied you. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her instead.” (15:2).
Samson said to them, “This time I will be blameless in doing harm to the Philistines.” (15:3).
Then Samson went out and caught three hundred foxes. And he took torches, turned the foxes tail-to-tail, and fastened a torch between each pair of tails. (15:4).
Then he lit the torches and released the foxes into the standing grain of the Philistines, burning up the piles of grain and the standing grain, as well as the vineyards and olive groves. (15:5).

“Who did this?” the Philistines demanded. “It was Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite,” they were told. “For his wife was given to his companion.” So the Philistines went up and burned her and her father to death. (15:6).
And Samson told them, “Because you have done this, I will not rest until I have taken vengeance upon you.” (15:7).
And he struck them ruthlessly with a great slaughter, and then went down and stayed in the cave at the rock of Etam. (15:8).
Then the Philistines went up, camped in Judah, and deployed themselves near the town of Lehi. (15:9).
“Why have you attacked us?” said the men of Judah. The Philistines replied, “We have come to arrest Samson and pay him back for what he has done to us.” (15:10).

In response, three thousand men of Judah went to the cave at the rock of Etam, and they asked Samson, “Do you not realize that the Philistines rule over us? What have you done to us?” “I have done to them what they did to me,” he replied. (15:11).
But they said to him, “We have come down to arrest you and hand you over to the Philistines.” Samson replied, “Swear to me that you will not kill me yourselves.” (15:12).
“No,” they answered, “we will not kill you, but we will tie you up securely and hand you over to them.” So they bound him with two new ropes and led him up from the rock. (15:13).

When Samson arrived in Lehi, the Philistines came out shouting against him. And the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him. The ropes on his arms became like burnt flax, and the bonds broke loose from his hands. (15:14).
He found the fresh jawbone of a donkey, reached out his hand and took it, and struck down a thousand men. (15:15).
Then Samson said: “With the jawbone of a donkey I have piled them into heaps. With the jawbone of a donkey I have slain a thousand men.” (15:16).
And when Samson had finished speaking, he cast the jawbone from his hand; and he named that place Ramath-lehi. (15:17).

And being very thirsty, Samson cried out to the LORD, “You have accomplished this great deliverance through Your servant. Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?” (15:18).

So God opened up the hollow place in Lehi, and water came out of it. When Samson drank, his strength returned, and he was revived. That is why he named it En-hakkore, and it remains in Lehi to this day. (15:19).
And Samson judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines. (15:20).
crossRefs: Judges 14:19-20: Samson's wife is given to the companion who had been his best man, which sets this chapter going.
Deuteronomy 32:35: Vengeance is Mine and recompense, for the time when their foot shall slip.
Exodus 22:6: Whoever starts a fire that spreads into standing grain must make full restitution for what is burned.
Judges 3:31: Shamgar son of Anath struck down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad and saved Israel.
Genesis 21:19: God opens Hagar's eyes and she sees a well of water, and she gives the boy a drink.

translationNotes.note: One Hebrew word covers both the fox and the jackal, and translators have to choose. Jackals run in packs and scavenge around towns and ruins, which makes taking them in numbers plausible in a way that trapping three hundred solitary foxes is not. Scripture uses the same word for the animals that haunt a ruined city (Lamentations 5:18) and that feed on the bodies of the fallen (Psalm 63:10). Tied tail to tail in pairs, three hundred animals carry a hundred and fifty torches.

translationNotes.term: The standing grain, the vineyards and olive groves
translationNotes.note: This is the destruction of an entire year in one night, at the worst possible moment. Wheat was cut with a hand sickle, bound, and stacked in the field before threshing, so verse 5 names both the cut stacks and the grain still standing. The vines and olives are worse: they are not an annual crop but decades of capital, and a young olive tree takes years to come into full bearing.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֶחִי (Lechi) - Hebrew: עֵין הַקּוֹרֵא (Ein ha-Qore)
translationNotes.note: All three names are made in the chapter itself. Lehi means jawbone, Ramath-lehi means the height of the jawbone, and En-hakkore means the spring of the one who called. The pattern of naming a place after what happened there runs through the whole Old Testament, and it is how a landscape kept its history when almost nobody could read.

translationNotes.term: The ropes became like burnt flax
translationNotes.note: Cord was spun from flax fibre or palm fibre and laid up into rope, and the text stresses that these two were new, at full strength. Flax that has been through a fire keeps its shape until it is touched and then falls apart. The verb used of the Spirit here and in Judges 14:6 and 14:19 is tsalach, to rush or break in on someone, not a gentle arrival.

Circumcision on the eighth day was the physical sign of the covenant made with Abraham (Genesis 17:10-14). It was not unique to Israel; Jeremiah 9:25-26 lists Egypt, Edom, Ammon, Moab, and the desert peoples alongside Judah as circumcised in the flesh. The Philistines, who had come to the coast from across the sea, did not practise it, which is why the word becomes the standing insult for them specifically, in Judges 14:3 and in David's question at the Valley of Elah in 1 Samuel 17:26.

stories.keyTakeaway: Samson's wife is given to another man, prompting him to burn the Philistines' crops with foxes; when they retaliate by killing his wife, he slaughters many of them and hides in a cave. Judah binds him and hands him over to the Philistines, but the Spirit of the LORD empowers him to break free and kill a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone; God provides water when he nearly dies of thirst.

stories.title: 🦁 Judges 16
summaryBullets: One day Samson went to Gaza, where he saw a prostitute and went in to spend the night with her. (16:1).

When the Gazites heard that Samson was there, they surrounded that place and lay in wait for him all night at the city gate. They were quiet throughout the night, saying, “Let us wait until dawn; then we will kill him.” (16:2).

But Samson lay there only until midnight, when he got up, took hold of the doors of the city gate and both gateposts, and pulled them out, bar and all. Then he put them on his shoulders and took them to the top of the mountain overlooking Hebron. (16:3).
Some time later, Samson fell in love with a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah. (16:4).

The lords of the Philistines went to her and said, “Entice him and find out the source of his great strength and how we can overpower him to tie him up and subdue him. Then each one of us will give you eleven hundred shekels of silver.” (16:5).
So Delilah said to Samson, “Please tell me the source of your great strength and how you can be tied up and subdued.” (16:6).
Samson told her, “If they tie me up with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, I will become as weak as any other man.” (16:7).
So the lords of the Philistines brought her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she tied him up with them. (16:8).

While the men were hidden in her room, she called out, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” But he snapped the bowstrings like a strand of yarn seared by a flame. So the source of his strength remained unknown. (16:9).
Then Delilah said to Samson, “You have mocked me and lied to me! Now please tell me how you can be tied up.” (16:10).
He replied, “If they tie me up with new ropes that have never been used, I will become as weak as any other man.” (16:11).

So Delilah took new ropes, tied him up with them, and called out, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” But while the men were hidden in her room, he snapped the ropes off his arms like they were threads. (16:12).

Then Delilah said to Samson, “You have mocked me and lied to me all along! Tell me how you can be tied up.” He told her, “If you weave the seven braids of my head into the web of a loom and tighten it with a pin, I will become as weak as any other man.” (16:13).

So while he slept, Delilah took the seven braids of his hair and wove them into the web.Then she tightened [it] with a pin and called to him, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” But he awoke from his sleep and pulled out the pin with the loom and the web. (16:14).
“How can you say, ‘I love you,’” she asked, “when your heart is not with me? This is the third time you have mocked me and failed to reveal to me the source of your great strength!” (16:15).
Finally, after she had pressed him daily with her words and pleaded until he was sick to death, (16:16).

Samson told her all that was in his heart: “My hair has never been cut, because I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother’s womb. If I am shaved, my strength will leave me, and I will become as weak as any other man.” (16:17).

When Delilah realized that he had revealed to her all that was in his heart, she sent this message to the lords of the Philistines: “Come up once more, for he has revealed to me all that is in his heart.” Then the lords of the Philistines came to her, bringing the money in their hands. (16:18).
And having lulled him to sleep on her lap, she called a man to shave off the seven braids of his head. In this way she began to subdue him, and his strength left him. (16:19).

Then she called out, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” When Samson awoke from his sleep, he thought, “I will escape as I did before and shake myself free.” But he did not know that the LORD had departed from him. (16:20).
Then the Philistines seized him, gouged out his eyes, and brought him down to Gaza, where he was bound with bronze shackles and forced to grind grain in the prison. (16:21).
However, the hair of his head began to grow back after it had been shaved. (16:22).
Now the lords of the Philistines gathered together to offer a great sacrifice to their god Dagon. They rejoiced and said, “Our god has delivered Samson our enemy into our hands.” (16:23).
And when the people saw him, they praised their god, saying: “Our god has delivered into our hands our enemy who destroyed our land and multiplied our dead.” (16:24).
And while their hearts were merry, they said, “Call for Samson to entertain us.” So they called Samson out of the prison to entertain them. And they stationed him between the pillars. (16:25).
Samson said to the servant who held his hand, “Lead me where I can feel the pillars supporting the temple, so I can lean against them.” (16:26).
Now the temple was full of men and women; all the lords of the Philistines were there, and about three thousand men and women were on the roof watching Samson entertain them. (16:27).
Then Samson called out to the LORD: “O Lord GOD, please remember me. Strengthen me, O God, just once more, so that with one vengeful blow I may pay back the Philistines for my two eyes.” (16:28).
And Samson reached out for the two central pillars supporting the temple. Bracing himself against them with his right hand on one pillar and his left hand on the other, (16:29).

Samson said, “Let me die with the Philistines.” Then he pushed with all his might, and the temple fell on the lords and all the people in it. So in his death he killed more than he had killed in his life. (16:30).
Then Samson’s brothers and his father’s family came down, carried him back, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah. And he had judged Israel twenty years. (16:31).
crossRefs: Judges 13:5: The child is to be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and no razor is to come on his head.
Numbers 6:5: All the days of his vow no razor shall touch his head; he shall let the locks of his hair grow long.
1 Samuel 5:1-5: The ark is set in Dagon's temple at Ashdod, and the image falls with its head and hands broken off.
Exodus 11:5: The firstborn of the slave girl who is behind the handmill, named as the lowest place in a household.
Hebrews 11:32-34: Samson is named among those who through faith were made strong out of weakness.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁעַר הָעִיר (shaar ha-ir), the city gate
translationNotes.note: Gaza was the southernmost of the five Philistine cities, on the coast road running down to Egypt. The gate was the single heaviest and most valuable piece of a town's defence: two leaves of timber plated or braced, hung on posts sunk into the ground, with a bar dropped across at dusk. Verse 3 has Samson pull out the doors, both posts and the bar together and carry them to a hill facing Hebron, which is roughly forty miles away and three thousand feet higher. The town wakes up with no gate.

Verse 23 names the god the Philistines credit with handing Samson over. Dagon had temples at Gaza and at Ashdod, and his name matches the Hebrew word for grain, dagan; two Israelite towns are called Beth-dagon, house of Dagon (Joshua 15:41, 19:27), which shows how far his worship reached. 1 Samuel 5:2-5 records what happened to his image at Ashdod when the captured ark was set beside it: it fell face down twice, and the second time its head and both hands were broken off on the threshold.

translationNotes.term: The two pillars of the house
translationNotes.note: Verse 27 puts about three thousand men and women on the roof watching, and verses 26 and 29 have Samson set his hands on the two central pillars the building rested on. Philistine temples of this kind have been dug up: the one excavated at Tell Qasile, on the northern edge of modern Tel Aviv, has two stone bases for wooden roof pillars set close enough together for one man to reach both at once. Pull those and the roof comes down on everyone standing on it.

Verse 21 has the blinded Samson set to grind in the prison. Daily flour was made by hand between two stones, hours of work every morning, and it was the job of women and slaves; Exodus 11:5 uses the slave girl at the mill as the picture of the very bottom of a household. Putting a captured champion on the mill was a deliberate public humiliation, not just forced labour.

Verse 5 has each of the five Philistine lords offer Delilah 1,100 pieces of silver, so 5,500 in all. Judges 17:10 hires a Levite for ten shekels of silver a year with food and clothing, which puts the offer at several lifetimes of wages. By weight, at about 0.4 ounces a shekel, it is roughly 140 pounds of silver.

stories.keyTakeaway: Samson visits a prostitute in Gaza and tears out the city gates; later, Delilah deceives him into revealing that his strength comes from his uncut hair, and after the Philistines shave his head and blind him, he prays for strength one final time and pulls down the temple, killing himself and thousands of Philistines.

stories.title: ⚖️ Judges 17
summaryBullets: Now a man named Micah from the hill country of Ephraim (17:1).

said to his mother, “The eleven hundred shekels of silver that were taken from you and about which I heard you utter a curse— I have the silver here with me; I took it.” Then his mother said, “Blessed be my son by the LORD!” (17:2).

And when he had returned the eleven hundred shekels of silver to his mother, she said, “I wholly dedicate the silver to the LORD for my son’s benefit, to make a graven image and a molten idol. Therefore I will now return it to you.” (17:3).

So he returned the silver to his mother, and she took two hundred shekels of silver and gave them to a silversmith, who made them into a graven image and a molten idol. And they were placed in the house of Micah. (17:4).
Now this man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and some household idols, and ordained one of his sons as his priest. (17:5).
In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes. (17:6).
And there was a young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah who had been residing within the clan of Judah. (17:7).
This man left the city of Bethlehem in Judah to settle where he could find a place. And as he traveled, he came to Micah’s house in the hill country of Ephraim. (17:8).
“Where are you from?” Micah asked him. “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah,” he replied, “and I am on my way to settle wherever I can find a place.” (17:9).
“Stay with me,” Micah said to him, “and be my father and priest, and I will give you ten shekels of silver per year, a suit of clothes, and your provisions.” So the Levite went in (17:10).
and agreed to stay with him, and the young man became like a son to Micah. (17:11).
Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest and lived in his house. (17:12).
Then Micah said, “Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because a Levite has become my priest.” (17:13).
crossRefs: Exodus 20:4-6: You shall not make for yourself a carved image or any likeness of what is in heaven or on earth, or bow down to them.
Deuteronomy 12:8: You shall not do as we are doing here today, everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes.
Numbers 3:5-10: The Levites are given to Aaron and his sons; any outsider who comes near the priesthood is to be put to death.
Deuteronomy 18:1-8: The Levites have no allotment among their brothers, and a Levite may come to the place the LORD chooses and minister there.
Exodus 28:6-30: The ephod made for the high priest, with the breastpiece of judgment and the Urim and Thummim.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פֶּסֶל (pesel), a hewn image - מַסֵּכָה (massekah), a poured image
translationNotes.note: Two different manufacturing methods, named separately because the law names both. A pesel is carved, from the verb to hew, usually in wood or stone; a massekah is cast, from the verb to pour, in molten metal over a core. Deuteronomy 27:15 puts a public curse on the man who makes either one, and Exodus 20:4 forbids them outright. Verse 3 is the sting of this chapter: the silver is dedicated to the LORD, by name, and then spent on exactly what He forbade.

Verse 5 has Micah make an ephod and teraphim for his private shrine. Teraphim are household images, kept in the home rather than at a sanctuary, and Scripture shows them used for divination (Ezekiel 21:21) and treated as valuable enough to steal: Rachel takes Laban's and hides them in a camel saddle (Genesis 31:19, 34). At least some were man-sized, since Michal lays one in David's bed to pass for a sleeping man (1 Samuel 19:13). Josiah swept them out of Judah along with the mediums and the idols (2 Kings 23:24).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִלֵּא יַד (mille yad), to fill the hand
translationNotes.note: The word translated ordained in verses 5 and 12 is literally filled his hand, and it is the fixed technical phrase for installing a priest, used of Aaron and his sons at Exodus 28:41 and 29:9. It carries the sense of putting the office, and the income, into a man's hands. Micah performs the rite on his own son, and then on a passing Levite, in a private house, with no authority to do either.

The tribe of Levi got no territory. It was given forty-eight towns scattered through the other tribes, and it lived on the tithes and the offerings brought to the sanctuary (Numbers 18:21-24, Joshua 21:41). Deuteronomy 18:6-8 gives a Levite the right to leave his town, come to the place the LORD chooses, and serve there on equal terms. Verses 7 to 13 show what happens when that system stops working: a young Levite from Bethlehem is on the road looking for somewhere to live, and takes a job as a private household priest for wages.

Verse 10 sets the Levite's terms: ten shekels of silver a year, a suit of clothes, and his food. That is about four ounces of silver annually, and it is one of the few plain wage figures in the Old Testament, useful for reading every other price in Scripture. The Levite takes a private household job because the arrangement God set up for his tribe had stopped working.

stories.keyTakeaway: Micah restores stolen silver to his mother, who uses part of it to make a silver idol for his shrine; he then hires a young Levite from Bethlehem as his priest, believing this will bring God's blessing.

stories.title: ⚖️ Judges 18
summaryBullets: In those days there was no king in Israel, and the tribe of the Danites was looking for territory to occupy. For up to that time they had not come into an inheritance among the tribes of Israel. (18:1).

So the Danites sent out five men from their clans, men of valor from Zorah and Eshtaol, to spy out the land and explore it. “Go and explore the land,” they told them. The men entered the hill country of Ephraim and came to the house of Micah, where they spent the night. (18:2).

And while they were near Micah’s house, they recognized the voice of the young Levite; so they went over and asked him, “Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? Why are you here?” (18:3).
“Micah has done this and that for me,” he replied, “and he has hired me to be his priest.” (18:4).
Then they said to him, “Please inquire of God to determine whether we will have a successful journey.” (18:5).
And the priest told them, “Go in peace. The LORD is watching over your journey.” (18:6).

So the five men departed and came to Laish, where they saw that the people were living securely, like the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting. There was nothing lacking in the land and no oppressive ruler. And they were far away from the Sidonians and had no alliance with anyone. (18:7).
When the men returned to Zorah and Eshtaol, their brothers asked them, “What did you find?” (18:8).
They answered, “Come on, let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and it is very good. Why would you fail to act? Do not hesitate to go there and take possession of the land! (18:9).
When you enter, you will come to an unsuspecting people and a spacious land, for God has delivered it into your hand. It is a place where nothing on earth is lacking.” (18:10).
So six hundred Danites departed from Zorah and Eshtaol, armed with weapons of war. (18:11).
They went up and camped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. That is why the place west of Kiriath-jearim is called Mahaneh-dan to this day. (18:12).
And from there they traveled to the hill country of Ephraim and came to Micah’s house. (18:13).

Then the five men who had gone to spy out the land of Laish said to their brothers, “Did you know that one of these houses has an ephod, household gods, a graven image, and a molten idol? Now think about what you should do.” (18:14).
So they turned aside there and went to the home of the young Levite, the house of Micah, and greeted him. (18:15).
The six hundred Danites stood at the entrance of the gate, armed with their weapons of war. (18:16).

And the five men who had gone to spy out the land went inside and took the graven image, the ephod, the household idols, and the molten idol, while the priest stood at the entrance of the gate with the six hundred armed men. (18:17).
When they entered Micah’s house and took the graven image, the ephod, the household idols, and the molten idol, the priest said to them, “What are you doing?” (18:18).

“Be quiet,” they told him. “Put your hand over your mouth and come with us and be a father and a priest to us. Is it better for you to be a priest for the house of one person or a priest for a tribe and family in Israel?” (18:19).
So the priest was glad and took the ephod, the household idols, and the graven image, and went with the people. (18:20).
Putting their small children, their livestock, and their possessions in front of them, they turned and departed. (18:21).
After they were some distance from Micah’s house, the men in the houses near Micah’s house mobilized and overtook the Danites. (18:22).
When they called out after them, the Danites turned to face them and said to Micah, “What is the matter with you that you have called out such a company?” (18:23).
He replied, “You took the gods I had made, and my priest, and went away. What else do I have? How can you say to me, ‘What is the matter with you?’” (18:24).
The Danites said to him, “Do not raise your voice against us, or angry men will attack you, and you and your family will lose your lives.” (18:25).
So the Danites went on their way, and Micah turned to go back home, because he saw that they were too strong for him. (18:26).
After they had taken Micah’s idols and his priest, they went to Laish, to a quiet and unsuspecting people, and they struck them with their swords and burned down the city. (18:27).
There was no one to deliver them, because the city was far from Sidon and had no alliance with anyone; it was in a valley near Beth-rehob. And the Danites rebuilt the city and lived there. (18:28).
They named it Dan, after their forefather Dan, who was born to Israel — though the city was formerly named Laish. (18:29).
The Danites set up idols for themselves, and Jonathan son of Gershom, the son of Moses, and his sons were priests for the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land. (18:30).
So they set up for themselves Micah’s graven image, and it was there the whole time the house of God was in Shiloh. (18:31).
crossRefs: Joshua 19:40-48: Dan's allotted territory on the coastal plain, and the tribe going up to fight Leshem and settling there.
Judges 1:34: The Amorites pressed the people of Dan back into the hill country and would not let them come down to the plain.
Deuteronomy 12:5-7: You shall seek the place the LORD your God chooses out of all your tribes, and go there.
1 Kings 12:28-30: Jeroboam sets one golden calf at Bethel and one at Dan, and the people go as far as Dan to worship.
Jeremiah 8:16: The snorting of their horses is heard from Dan, and the whole land trembles at the sound.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲגוּרִים כְּלֵי מִלְחָמָה (chagurim kele milchamah), girded with weapons of war
translationNotes.note: Verses 11 and 16 count the fighting men who move north as six hundred, with the families and livestock behind them and the children in front (verse 21). This is a whole clan on the move under an armed screen, not a raiding party. Six hundred is the standing size of a body of men in this period: David's band settles at six hundred (1 Samuel 23:13), and six hundred Benjaminites survive at the rock of Rimmon (20:47).

translationNotes.term: Priest to a tribe rather than to one house
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָב וְכֹהֵן (av ve-kohen), a father and a priest
translationNotes.note: Verse 19 offers the Levite a promotion and he takes it: be priest to a tribe and a clan in Israel instead of to one man's household. The offer is put to him with a hand over his mouth and six hundred armed men at the gate, and verse 20 says his heart was glad. Priesthood here has become a post with a salary and a career, which is the point the chapter is making about the period.

The book waits until verse 30 to name the priest, and the name lands hard: Jonathan son of Gershom, the son of Moses. Gershom was Moses' firstborn, born in Midian (Exodus 2:22, 18:3). So the shrine at Dan, built around stolen idols, is served by Moses' own grandson and by his sons after him, and the verse says the line held the post until the captivity of the land.

The town lay at the northern springs that feed the Jordan, under Mount Hermon, isolated from Sidon and with no defence treaty (verses 7 and 28). Renamed Dan, it becomes the northern marker of the whole land in the phrase from Dan to Beersheba, and centuries later Jeroboam puts one of his golden calves there (1 Kings 12:29). An Aramaic victory inscription naming the house of David was found at the site in 1993.

stories.keyTakeaway: Five Danite spies scout Laish, approve it as a settlement, and the tribe sends six hundred armed men who seize Micah's priest and religious objects, intimidate Micah into silence, then conquer Laish and rename it Dan.

stories.title: ⚖️ Judges 19
summaryBullets: Now in those days, when there was no king in Israel, a Levite who lived in the remote hill country of Ephraim took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah. (19:1).
But she was unfaithful to him and left him to return to her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah. After she had been there four months, (19:2).

her husband got up and went after her to speak kindly to her and bring her back, taking his servant and a pair of donkeys. So the girl brought him into her father’s house, and when her father saw him, he gladly welcomed him. (19:3).
His father-in-law, the girl’s father, persuaded him to stay, so he remained with him three days, eating, drinking, and lodging there. (19:4).
On the fourth day, they got up early in the morning and prepared to depart, but the girl’s father said to his son-in-law, “Refresh your heart with a morsel of bread, and then you can go.” (19:5).
So they sat down and the two of them ate and drank together. Then the girl’s father said to the man, “Please agree to stay overnight and let your heart be merry.” (19:6).
The man got up to depart, but his father-in-law persuaded him, so he stayed there that night. (19:7).
On the fifth day, he got up early in the morning to depart, but the girl’s father said, “Please refresh your heart.” So they waited until late afternoon and the two of them ate. (19:8).

When the man got up to depart with his concubine and his servant, his father-in-law, the girl’s father, said to him, “Look, the day is drawing to a close. Please spend the night. See, the day is almost over. Spend the night here, that your heart may be merry. Then you can get up early tomorrow for your journey home.” (19:9).
But the man was unwilling to spend the night. He got up and departed, and arrived opposite Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), with his two saddled donkeys and his concubine. (19:10).
When they were near Jebus and the day was almost gone, the servant said to his master, “Please, let us stop at this Jebusite city and spend the night here.” (19:11).
But his master replied, “We will not turn aside to the city of foreigners, where there are no Israelites. We will go on to Gibeah.” (19:12).
He continued, “Come, let us try to reach one of these towns to spend the night in Gibeah or Ramah.” (19:13).
So they continued on their journey, and the sun set as they neared Gibeah in Benjamin. (19:14).
They stopped to go in and lodge in Gibeah. The Levite went in and sat down in the city square, but no one would take them into his home for the night. (19:15).
That evening an old man from the hill country of Ephraim, who was residing in Gibeah (the men of that place were Benjamites), came in from his work in the field. (19:16).
When he looked up and saw the traveler in the city square, the old man asked, “Where are you going, and where have you come from?” (19:17).

The Levite replied, “We are traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to the remote hill country of Ephraim, where I am from. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am going to the house of the LORD; but no one has taken me into his home, (19:18).
even though there is both straw and feed for our donkeys, and bread and wine for me and the maidservant and young man with me. There is nothing that we, your servants, lack.” (19:19).
“Peace to you,” said the old man. “Let me supply everything you need. Only do not spend the night in the square.” (19:20).
So he brought him to his house and fed his donkeys. And they washed their feet and ate and drank. (19:21).

While they were enjoying themselves, suddenly the wicked men of the city surrounded the house. Pounding on the door, they said to the old man who owned the house, “Bring out the man who came to your house, so we can have relations with him!” (19:22).
The owner of the house went out and said to them, “No, my brothers, do not do this wicked thing! After all, this man is a guest in my house. Do not commit this outrage. (19:23).
Look, let me bring out my virgin daughter and the man’s concubine, and you can use them and do with them as you wish. But do not do such a vile thing to this man.” (19:24).
But the men would not listen to him. So the Levite took his concubine and sent her outside to them, and they raped her and abused her throughout the night, and at dawn they let her go. (19:25).
Early that morning, the woman went back to the house where her master was staying, collapsed at the doorway, and lay there until it was light. (19:26).

In the morning, when her master got up and opened the doors of the house to go out on his journey, there was his concubine, collapsed in the doorway of the house, with her hands on the threshold. (19:27).
“Get up,” he told her. “Let us go.” But there was no response. So the man put her on his donkey and set out for home. (19:28).
When he reached his house, he picked up a knife, took hold of his concubine, cut her limb by limb into twelve pieces, and sent her throughout the territory of Israel. (19:29).
And everyone who saw it said, “Nothing like this has been seen or done from the day the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt until this day. Think it over, take counsel, and speak up!” (19:30).
crossRefs: Genesis 19:1-11: The men of Sodom surround Lot's house and demand the visitors, and Lot offers them his daughters.
Genesis 18:1-8: Abraham runs to meet three men, has their feet washed, and sets a meal before them under the tree.
Deuteronomy 22:25-27: The law for the man who seizes a betrothed woman in the open country and forces her.
Hosea 9:9: They have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah; He will remember their iniquity.
Hosea 10:9: From the days of Gibeah you have sinned, O Israel; there they have continued.

translationNotes.note: A pilegesh was a secondary wife: a real and recognised marriage, but without the standing, the settlement or the family backing of a full wife, and her children ranked below the wife's. Verses 3 to 9 show the relationship for what it legally was, with the Levite going to her father's house and being kept there five days as a son-in-law. The law protects such a woman in Exodus 21:7-11, which requires that her food, clothing and marital rights not be reduced, and lets her go free if they are.

A Benjamite town on the central ridge road about three miles north of Jerusalem, which is why the Levite passes over Jebusite Jerusalem to reach it (verses 11 and 12). He chooses the Israelite town over the foreign one on purpose. Gibeah is later Saul's home and seat (1 Samuel 10:26, 11:4), and Hosea twice uses its name as a byword for how low Israel went.

translationNotes.term: No one took them into his house
translationNotes.note: Verse 15 has the travellers sit in the open square of the town because nobody offers them shelter, and that is the first thing wrong in the chapter. In a country with no inns, taking in a traveller before dark was a duty every household understood; Abraham runs to do it in Genesis 18. The old man who finally takes them in is not from Gibeah at all, but from Ephraim (verse 16).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֵתַח (netach), a piece of a butchered carcass
translationNotes.note: Verse 29 uses the vocabulary of butchering a sacrifice, the word for the joints an animal is cut into. What the Levite sends round the tribes is a summons that cannot be filed away or ignored, and it works: chapter 20 opens with the whole nation assembled. Saul does the same thing with a yoke of oxen when he calls out the militia for Jabesh-gilead and says this is what will be done to the oxen of any man who does not come (1 Samuel 11:7).

stories.keyTakeaway: A Levite retrieves his unfaithful concubine from Bethlehem, and after lingering with her father, they travel to Gibeah where wicked men of the city gang-rape her through the night; the Levite cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel.

stories.title: ⚖️ Judges 20
summaryBullets: Then all the Israelites from Dan to Beersheba and from the land of Gilead came out, and the congregation assembled as one man before the LORD at Mizpah. (20:1).
The leaders of all the people and all the tribes of Israel presented themselves in the assembly of God’s people: 400,000 men on foot, armed with swords. (20:2).
(Meanwhile the Benjamites heard that the Israelites had gone up to Mizpah.) And the Israelites asked, “Tell us, how did this wicked thing happen?” (20:3).
So the Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, answered: “I and my concubine came to Gibeah in Benjamin to spend the night. (20:4).
And during the night, the men of Gibeah rose up against me and surrounded the house. They intended to kill me, but they abused my concubine, and she died. (20:5).
Then I took my concubine, cut her into pieces, and sent her throughout the land of Israel’s inheritance, because they had committed a lewd and disgraceful act in Israel. (20:6).
Behold, all you Israelites, give your advice and verdict here and now.” (20:7).
Then all the people stood as one man and said, “Not one of us will return to his tent or to his house. (20:8).
Now this is what we will do to Gibeah: We will go against it as the lot dictates. (20:9).

We will take ten men out of every hundred from all the tribes of Israel, and a hundred out of every thousand, and a thousand out of every ten thousand, to supply provisions for the army when they go to Gibeah in Benjamin to punish them for the atrocity they have committed in Israel.” (20:10).
So all the men of Israel gathered as one man, united against the city. (20:11).
And the tribes of Israel sent men throughout the tribe of Benjamin, saying, “What is this wickedness that has occurred among you? (20:12).
Hand over the wicked men of Gibeah so we can put them to death and purge Israel of this evil.” But the Benjamites refused to heed the voice of their fellow Israelites. (20:13).
And from their cities they came together at Gibeah to go out and fight against the Israelites. (20:14).
On that day the Benjamites mobilized 26,000 swordsmen from their cities, in addition to the 700 select men of Gibeah. (20:15).
Among all these soldiers there were 700 select left-handers, each of whom could sling a stone at a hair without missing. (20:16).
The Israelites, apart from Benjamin, mobilized 400,000 swordsmen, each one an experienced warrior. (20:17).
The Israelites set out, went up to Bethel, and inquired of God, “Who of us shall go up first to fight against the Benjamites?” “Judah will be first,” the LORD replied. (20:18).
The next morning the Israelites set out and camped near Gibeah. (20:19).
And the men of Israel went out to fight against Benjamin and took up their battle positions at Gibeah. (20:20).
And the Benjamites came out of Gibeah and cut down 22,000 Israelites on the battlefield that day. (20:21).
But the Israelite army took courage and again took their battle positions in the same place where they had arrayed themselves on the first day. (20:22).

They went up and wept before the LORD until evening, inquiring of Him, “Should we again draw near for battle against our brothers the Benjamites?” And the LORD answered, “Go up against them.” (20:23).
On the second day the Israelites advanced against the Benjamites. (20:24).
That same day the Benjamites came out against them from Gibeah and cut down another 18,000 Israelites, all of them armed with swords. (20:25).

Then the Israelites, all the people, went up to Bethel, where they sat weeping before the LORD. That day they fasted until evening and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings to the LORD. (20:26).
And the Israelites inquired of the LORD. (In those days the ark of the covenant of God was there, (20:27).

and Phinehas son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, served before it.) The Israelites asked, “Should we again go out to battle against our brothers the Benjamites, or should we stop?” The LORD answered, “Fight, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hand.” (20:28).
So Israel set up an ambush around Gibeah. (20:29).
On the third day the Israelites went up against the Benjamites and arrayed themselves against Gibeah as they had done before. (20:30).

The Benjamites came out against them and were drawn away from the city. They began to attack the people as before, killing about thirty men of Israel in the fields and on the roads, one of which led up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah. (20:31).
“We are defeating them as before,” said the Benjamites. But the Israelites said, “Let us retreat and draw them away from the city onto the roads.” (20:32).
So all the men of Israel got up from their places and arrayed themselves at Baal-tamar, and the Israelites in ambush charged from their positions west of Gibeah. (20:33).
Then 10,000 select men from all Israel made a frontal assault against Gibeah, and the battle was fierce. But the Benjamites did not realize that disaster was upon them. (20:34).
The LORD defeated Benjamin in the presence of Israel, and on that day the Israelites slaughtered 25,100 Benjamites, all armed with swords. (20:35).
Then the Benjamites realized they had been defeated. Now the men of Israel had retreated before Benjamin because they were relying on the ambush they had set against Gibeah. (20:36).
The men in ambush rushed suddenly against Gibeah; they advanced and put the whole city to the sword. (20:37).
The men of Israel had arranged a signal with the men in ambush: When they sent up a great cloud of smoke from the city, (20:38).

the men of Israel would turn in the battle. When the Benjamites had begun to strike them down, killing about thirty men of Israel, they said, “They are defeated before us as in the first battle.” (20:39).
But when the column of smoke began to go up from the city, the Benjamites looked behind them and saw the whole city going up in smoke. (20:40).
Then the men of Israel turned back on them, and the men of Benjamin were terrified when they realized that disaster had come upon them. (20:41).
So they fled before the men of Israel toward the wilderness, but the battle overtook them, and the men coming out of the cities struck them down there. (20:42).
They surrounded the Benjamites, pursued them, and easily overtook them in the vicinity of Gibeah on the east. (20:43).
And 18,000 Benjamites fell, all men of valor. (20:44).
Then the Benjamites turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon, and Israel cut down 5,000 men on the roads. And they overtook them at Gidom and struck down 2,000 more. (20:45).
That day 25,000 Benjamite swordsmen fell, all men of valor. (20:46).
But 600 men turned and fled into the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon, where they stayed four months. (20:47).

And the men of Israel turned back against the other Benjamites and put to the sword all the cities, including the animals and everything else they found. And they burned down all the cities in their path. (20:48).
