Deuteronomy 13:12-18: A town that has turned aside to serve other gods is to be struck down and its spoil burned in the open square.
Deuteronomy 17:2-7: The evil is to be purged from your midst, and the hand of the witnesses is first against the guilty.
Joshua 8:3-22: Joshua sets an ambush behind Ai and draws the defenders out with a feigned retreat.
Numbers 27:21: Israel inquires of God before the priest, the practice followed at Bethel in verses 27 and 28.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּאִישׁ אֶחָד (ke-ish echad), as one man
translationNotes.note: Verse 1 measures the muster by the two ends of the country, Dan in the far north under Hermon and Beersheba on the edge of the Negev, and adds Gilead across the Jordan. There is no king and no standing army; the tribes assemble themselves at Mizpah, a hilltop in Benjamin about eight miles north of Jerusalem, and act as one body. Samuel gathers the nation at the same place in 1 Samuel 7:5-6 and 10:17.

A sling is two cords on a leather pouch, whirled and released by letting one cord go. It was not a toy: armies fielded slingers as a standing arm, and the Assyrian relief panels of the siege of Lachish, cut for Sennacherib's palace and now in the British Museum, show them working the line alongside the archers. A stone thrown that way kills outright, which is what happens at 1 Samuel 17:49. Verse 16 says these seven hundred could sling at a hair and not miss.

Verses 27 and 28 mention almost in passing that the ark of the covenant was at Bethel and that Phinehas son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, was ministering before it. That dates the whole episode. Phinehas is the man who stopped the plague at Peor in Moses' own lifetime (Numbers 25:7-8), so this atrocity belongs near the start of the period of the judges, not at its end, even though the book places it last.

Verse 47 has six hundred Benjaminites hold out four months on a rock in the wilderness east of the hill country. Sela means a crag or cliff, not a boulder, and country like that is full of limestone spurs with caves and one approach, which is why fugitives head for them all through Scripture; David does the same at Adullam and En-gedi. Those six hundred men are the entire tribe of Benjamin that survives chapter 20, which is the problem chapter 21 exists to solve.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel assembles at Mizpah, hears the Levite's account of his concubine's rape and death in Gibeah, and demands Benjamin turn over the guilty men; when Benjamin refuses, Israel fights three battles against them, using an ambush on the third day to defeat Benjamin and destroy their towns, leaving only six hundred Benjamite survivors who flee to the rock of Rimmon.

stories.title: ⚖️ Judges 21
summaryBullets: Now the men of Israel had sworn an oath at Mizpah, saying, “Not one of us will give his daughter in marriage to a Benjamite.” (21:1).
So the people came to Bethel and sat there before God until evening, lifting up their voices and weeping bitterly. (21:2).
“Why, O LORD God of Israel,” they cried out, “has this happened in Israel? Today in Israel one tribe is missing!” (21:3).
The next day the people got up early, built an altar there, and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings. (21:4).

The Israelites asked, “Who among all the tribes of Israel did not come to the assembly before the LORD?” For they had taken a solemn oath that anyone who failed to come up before the LORD at Mizpah would surely be put to death. (21:5).
And the Israelites grieved for their brothers, the Benjamites, and said, “Today a tribe is cut off from Israel. (21:6).
What should we do about wives for the survivors, since we have sworn by the LORD not to give them our daughters in marriage?” (21:7).
So they asked, “Which one of the tribes of Israel failed to come up before the LORD at Mizpah?” And, in fact, no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp for the assembly. (21:8).
For when the people were counted, none of the residents of Jabesh-gilead were there. (21:9).
So the congregation sent 12,000 of their most valiant men and commanded them: “Go and put to the sword those living in Jabesh-gilead, including women and children. (21:10).
This is what you are to do: Devote to destruction every male, as well as every female who has had relations with a man.” (21:11).
So they found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead four hundred young women who had not had relations with a man, and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh in the land of Canaan. (21:12).
Then the whole congregation sent a message of peace to the Benjamites who were at the rock of Rimmon. (21:13).
And at that time the Benjamites returned and were given the women who were spared from Jabesh-gilead. But there were not enough women for all of them. (21:14).
The people grieved for Benjamin, because the LORD had made a void in the tribes of Israel. (21:15).
Then the elders of the congregation said, “What should we do about wives for those who remain, since the women of Benjamin have been destroyed?” (21:16).
They added, “There must be heirs for the survivors of Benjamin, so that a tribe of Israel will not be wiped out. (21:17).
But we cannot give them our daughters as wives.” For the Israelites had sworn, “Cursed is he who gives a wife to a Benjamite.” (21:18).
“But look,” they said, “there is a yearly feast to the LORD in Shiloh, which is north of Bethel east of the road that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah.” (21:19).
So they commanded the Benjamites: “Go, hide in the vineyards (21:20).

and watch. When you see the daughters of Shiloh come out to perform their dances, each of you is to come out of the vineyards, catch for himself a wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin. (21:21).

When their fathers or brothers come to us to complain, we will tell them, ‘Do us a favor by helping them, since we did not get wives for each of them in the war. Since you did not actually give them your daughters, you have no guilt.’” (21:22).

The Benjamites did as instructed and carried away the number of women they needed from the dancers they caught. They went back to their own inheritance, rebuilt their cities, and settled in them. (21:23).
And at that time, each of the Israelites returned from there to his own tribe and clan, each to his own inheritance. (21:24).
In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes. (21:25).
crossRefs: Judges 20:47-48: Six hundred men escape to the rock of Rimmon while every town of Benjamin is put to the sword and burned.
Numbers 31:15-18: The young women who had not known a man are kept alive out of Midian.
Judges 11:30-39: Jephthah's vow and how he kept it, another oath honoured to the letter at terrible cost.
1 Samuel 11:1-11: Saul, himself a Benjamite, marches all night to rescue Jabesh-gilead, the town struck here.
Deuteronomy 23:21-23: If you make a vow to the LORD, do not delay to fulfil it, for He will surely require it of you.

translationNotes.note: This chapter runs on two oaths sworn in the heat of the assembly, and Israel treats both as unbreakable. Verse 1 swears that no one will give a daughter to a Benjaminite; verse 5 swears death on any town that failed to turn up. A shevuah is a sworn oath, stronger than a vow, and Numbers 30:2 binds a man to everything that comes out of his mouth. The tribes will not simply repent of the oath, so they spend the rest of the chapter finding ways round it.

Verses 8 to 12 destroy an Israelite town under the ban for not sending men to the assembly, and spare four hundred unmarried women out of it. The town sits east of the Jordan in Gilead. Two later episodes turn on this: Saul's first act as king is to march overnight and break the Ammonite siege of Jabesh-gilead (1 Samuel 11:1-11), and when he dies it is the men of Jabesh-gilead who travel all night to take his body off the wall of Beth-shan and bury him (1 Samuel 31:11-13).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָטַף (chataf), to snatch or catch
translationNotes.note: Verses 20 to 23 solve the oath by arranging an abduction: the surviving Benjaminites lie in the vineyards and each carries off a woman from the dance, and the elders undertake to square it with the fathers and brothers afterwards. The law they are working around is the one they swore themselves, since the fathers cannot be said to have given their daughters if the daughters were taken. Verse 25 closes the book on the sentence it has repeated four times: in those days there was no king in Israel, and everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

Verses 19 to 21 describe a yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh where the young women came out to dance in the vineyards, and the chapter gives directions to the place: north of Bethel, east of the road from Bethel to Shechem, south of Lebonah. Vineyard dances at a harvest feast were a normal part of the year. The chapter uses that ordinary festival as cover for carrying women off, and reports it without approving it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel grieves over Benjamin's near destruction and devises two plans to provide wives for the surviving Benjamites: first taking four hundred virgins from Jabesh Gilead, then instructing the Benjamites to seize young women dancing at the festival in Shiloh.

intro:
Judges does not name its author. Jewish tradition (preserved in the Talmud, Baba Bathra 14b-15a) attributes the book to the prophet Samuel, the last judge of Israel and the figure who anointed both Saul and David as kings. The composition dates to roughly 1045-1000 BC, between Saul's anointing (c. 1051 BC) and David's capture of Jerusalem (c. 1004 BC), placing it within Samuel's lifetime. Samuel was born in the hill country of Ephraim to Hannah, dedicated to God before his birth, and raised at the Tabernacle in Shiloh under Eli the high priest. He came from a Levite family (1 Chronicles 6:33-38), served as judge, prophet, and circuit rider between Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, and led Israel during the transition from the era of judges to the monarchy. The historical setting is the Iron Age I in Canaan, covering roughly the three-and-a-half centuries between Joshua's death (c. 1380 BC) and Samuel's day, with the Israelite tribes settled in a loose confederacy across the hill country, the Philistine sea peoples having recently arrived on the coastal plain, the Egyptian New Kingdom collapsing under the late Ramesside Pharaohs, the Hittite Empire destroyed in the Bronze Age collapse (c. 1180 BC), and the surrounding peoples (Moabites, Ammonites, Midianites, Amalekites, Aramaeans) pressing in against the unsettled tribes.

Judges is the seventh book of the Hebrew Bible and the second of the Former Prophets (Nevi'im Rishonim) in the Jewish canon. The Hebrew name Shoftim means "Judges" or "Rulers"; the English title comes from the Latin Vulgate Iudicum, via the Greek Septuagint Kritai (3rd century BC). Hebrew manuscript fragments of Judges were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the 2nd and 1st centuries BC.
